caveats: Workflow errored at its tail; paired cross-model refutation reached 2 of 6 intended clusters. Most findings carry single-model verification.
Findings pinned to corpus commit 9c715d7. Anything pushed since is unreviewed.

The ABAC/DCS architecture was authored concurrently with RL#1 (branched from the same base 5e76b96), not in response to it — dispositions of "open" reflect disjoint surfaces, not unaddressed feedback.

Count reconciliation: the RL#2 comment posted to issue #1 cited 84 confirmed; re-deriving the verdict-to-cluster join for this digest yields 85. The difference is one finding recovered by the join, not a changed judgment. This digest is authoritative for the per-finding record.

findings.relocated_class: Class A (enforcement asserted without a trust-plane locus) relocated, not killed: the kernel/PEP split addresses the symptom, but the authorization-bearing state becomes a TTL-scoped signed credential held and freshness-checked by an untrusted-adjacent plane (§3.1 state-store/lake), with the trust plane deliberately off the path (§7.2) — same structural shape at a new seam. Aggravated by §7.3, where the RLS backstop's SET LOCAL GUC inputs are asserted from that same cached context, so the two layers share an attribute-assertion path despite §7.3's independence claim.
findings.summary: The kernel-minted subject context is a TTL-scoped cached authorization held off the kernel hot path, contradicting the document's own 'no cached-allow', 'per-request evaluation', and 'kernel-mediated access' statements, with no revocation or drift-detection mechanism.
findings.evidence: §7.2: 'issued once per session/task and re-validated on TTL expiry or attribute drift, keeping the kernel off the per-query hot path' vs §1.2 'no grace mode, no cached-allow', §2.1 'per-request evaluation', §3.1 'the runtime touches state only through the kernel's decisions', and §9.2 'Kernel unreachable | Every PEP denies… a subject context past TTL is a denial' (which concedes that within TTL it does not deny). No mechanism is specified by which an off-hot-path PEP learns of attribute drift or revocation; no maximum TTL is stated anywhere; revocation latency therefore equals the TTL. Undercuts the AC-3(3)/AC-25 always-invoked reference-monitor property claimed in §15.
findings.recommendation: Either state the bounded cached-allow honestly (maximum TTL as a function of the declared lattice, stated revocation latency, §9.2 row rewritten, §1.2 and §2.1 amended) or restore always-invoked evaluation via a kernel-published epoch/generation counter the PEP must carry per transaction so drift fails closed. Add the TTL bound as a §9.1 boot check and a §12 vector.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
VERIFIED AGAINST TEXT — I tried to refute on four fronts and the finding survived three of them.

Refutation attempt 1 — "cached *attributes* ≠ cached *allow*." §7.2 calls the subject context "a short-lived, signed attribute snapshot," not a permit, and the per-query label predicates are still evaluated at query time (as they are in RLS). Under that reading §1.2's "no cached-allow" and §3's "the kernel is the only PDP" survive. This is the strongest defense available and it partly lands — the finding's framing overstates when it calls the context a "cached authorization" tout court. But it does not survive the document's own §9.2 row 1, which is the load-bearing text: "Kernel unreachable | Every PEP denies. No cached-allow; a subject context past TTL is a denial." The second clause contradicts the first. If the kernel is unreachable and the PEP still serves queries until TTL expiry, then not every PEP denies — the row concedes a window in which enforcement proceeds on kernel-independent state. That is the literal definition of a cached-allow window, written into the fail-closed matrix by the document itself. §7.2 states the intent plainly: "keeping the kernel off the per-query hot path."

Refutation attempt 2 — "addressed elsewhere in the corpus." I searched abac-dcs-architecture.md for TTL / cache / drift / revocation / epoch. The only adjacent material: (a) §4 rule 3 and §9.2 row 2, which bound *scheduled task identities* ("re-evaluate at fire time"; drift fails closed) — real coverage, but only for the task case, not the interactive session case §7.2 explicitly covers ("issued once per session/task"); (b) §5.1's "STIG-aligned session lifetimes," which bounds a session, not the subject-context TTL, and is an inherited operational pattern, not a stated maximum; (c) §17 Q4, which flags the subject-context *envelope* (JWT vs bespoke) as open — the format, explicitly not the TTL bound or the revocation semantics. Nowhere in the document is a maximum TTL stated, and nowhere is a mechanism specified by which an off-hot-path PEP learns of attribute drift or revocation. §7.2's phrase "re-validated on TTL expiry **or attribute drift**" is the exact seam: drift-triggered revalidation requires the PEP to learn of drift, which is impossible for a component the design has deliberately taken off the kernel path. Revocation latency therefore does equal the TTL, and the TTL is unbounded in the text.

Refutation attempt 3 — "YAGNI / rough-draft deferral." Rejected. This is not an unspecified implementation detail; it is a ratified decision (D9) that contradicts a ratified doctrine (§1.2, D10 "fail closed everywhere") and a conformance claim. §2.1 answers NIST SP 800-207 with "per-request evaluation" and answers DoDI 8520.04's "authorization at request time from digital policy rules" with "dynamic-access-native from birth." A session-scoped attribute snapshot evaluated off the kernel path is not per-request evaluation against the authoritative attribute service; it is periodic revalidation. The conformance-claim overreach is confirmed on the text, and conformance claims are exactly what a design doc is on the hook for.

Refutation attempt 4 — factual overreach in the finding. Partly lands: the finding cites "AC-3(3)/AC-25 always-invoked reference-monitor property claimed in §15." §15 does claim AC-3(3) (row: "Bell-LaPadula dominance at three layers") and SC-3, but AC-25 (reference monitor) appears nowhere in §15 or the document. The AC-25 half of that sentence is fabricated; the AC-3(3) half stands. This is a citation error inside the detail field, not a defect in the finding, and does not refute.

SHARPENING the finding (adjacent, same seam, arguably stronger than what was filed): §7.3 has the PEP supply subject attributes to RLS as per-transaction SET LOCAL GUCs, and §3.1 classifies state-store as "data plane, untrusted-adjacent like lake." So the Layer-3 backstop's decision inputs are asserted by Layer 2 from the same cached context. §7.3's claim "Disclosure requires Layer 2 and Layer 3 to fail identically — and they are implemented independently" is weakened accordingly: the layers are independent in *predicate implementation* but share a single *attribute assertion path*, and the freshness check on that path is performed by the untrusted-adjacent holder itself. That is the precise mechanism by which this is RL#1 Class A relocated rather than killed.

RL#1 disposition — RELOCATED, strictly. RL#1 Class A was "enforcement asserted without a trust-plane locus," with B2 (the hook-B disclosure gate running as local bindings inside the untrusted lake) as the flagship. This document performs the recommended redesign at the top level — kernel as sole PDP, split from enforcement, RLS backstop — which addresses the symptom. But §7.2 reintroduces the identical structural shape one layer down: the effective authorization state is a bearer artifact held, cached, and freshness-checked by an untrusted-adjacent component, with the trust plane deliberately absent from the path. RL#1 §6 named this exact relocation shape in advance ("a kernel-brokered write API that reintroduces a trust boundary at the API surface"). Same shape, new seam → relocated, not killed.

EXTERNAL FLOOR — false. Every remedy the finding names is inside the system's control and cheap at design stage: a stated maximum TTL as a function of the declared lattice (already a boot-checkable quantity per §9.1 item 7's instance-ceiling pattern), a kernel-published epoch/generation counter the PEP must carry per transaction so a stale generation fails closed, or the kernel bulk-decision API §7.2 already contemplates for the lake hot path. Nothing here terminates against an invariant outside the system. This is a patchable seam, and the fact that the measurement-driven bulk-decision option is already in the document (§7.2, §17 Q2) proves the seam is reachable.

SEVERITY — held at blocker. It is a design-level contradiction of a ratified doctrine (D10/§1.2), a ratified decision (D9), and a cited-standard conformance claim (§2.1, DoDI 8520.04 §3.4/§4.3); the resolution changes the hot-path architecture and the internal-credential envelope (§17 Q4), which is expensive to unwind once the kernel skeleton exists — the same "expensive after implementation starts" test RL#1 §5 applied to ADR-0004/0005. It is also independently derived by all three model families including a blind pass, which is evidence of a property of the design rather than reviewer echo. Recommend it be folded into the ADR-0005 (enforcement-locus / TCB boundary) successor rather than filed as a standalone patch, with §9.2 row 1 rewritten to state the bounded window honestly and a TTL/epoch bound added as a §9.1 boot check and a §12 conformance vector.

findings.relocated_class: Class A relocated to the state-store/RLS seam: trusted-plane enforcement (RLS predicates generated by trust-plane tooling) whose decision inputs (SET LOCAL subject-attribute GUCs) are computed and delivered by the untrusted plane with no trusted verification locus in between. RL#1 B2 placed the disclosure gate inside the untrusted lake; the response moved the enforcement point to PostgreSQL but left the input-trust boundary in the same structural position — enforcement point moved, class not killed.
findings.summary: No trusted component is specified between the untrusted PEP and PostgreSQL that verifies the signed subject context before the attribute GUCs are trusted, so a compromised PEP sets top-of-lattice attributes and RLS dutifully returns every row — Layer 3 is not independent of Layer 2.
findings.evidence: §7.3: 'Subject attributes arrive as per-transaction SET LOCAL GUCs' and 'Disclosure requires Layer 2 and Layer 3 to fail identically — and they are implemented independently.' The GUCs are issued by the database client, and the clients are the Layer-2 PEPs in untrusted-by-design containers. PostgreSQL cannot verify the snapshot signature; nothing states which role may set the GUCs, who validates audience/expiry, or how direct SQL self-assertion is denied. Connection architecture is itself still an open question.
findings.recommendation: Terminate the subject context inside the trust plane: a trusted connection broker (trust-plane, Rust) that is the only party permitted to issue the attribute SET LOCALs, or a SECURITY DEFINER/extension verification function owned by a role the service role cannot impersonate. State explicitly in §7.3 what makes Layer 3's inputs unforgeable by Layer 2.
findings.verifier_reasoning: Verified against the text; refutation attempts failed. (1) The apparent counter-evidence — abac §3.1 line 80 "kernel-mediated access to the state store" and container-arch principle 5 — is overridden by §7.2 line 186, which states the subject context is issued once per session/task "keeping the kernel off the per-query hot path," and by §17 Q3, which frames connection architecture as "per-service pools vs. a pooler," i.e. the services hold the PostgreSQL connections. Line 80's own closing clause is decision-mediation ("only through the kernel's decisions"), not data-path mediation. (2) container-arch §4 state-data ("access is SQL through layer-2 PEPs only") plus §2's inventory (runtime/lake/dreamer = "Untrusted by design") makes the untrusted plane the DB client, and therefore the party issuing SET LOCAL. (3) Every §7.3 hardening bullet (FORCE RLS, no BYPASSRLS, deny-all default, NOT NULL labels) constrains what the policy evaluates over, never who supplies the GUC values; PostgreSQL customized-option GUCs (dcs.*) are settable by any role absent a C extension declaring them superuser/restricted, and no such extension is specified anywhere in the corpus. (4) The §17 open questions do not cover it: Q3 defers connection architecture and Q4 defers the credential envelope, while §7.3's independence claim ("Disclosure requires Layer 2 and Layer 3 to fail identically — and they are implemented independently") is asserted as settled. Implementation independence is not input independence; Layer 3's sole inputs come from Layer 2. Additional aggravating evidence the finding did not cite: this is an internal contradiction, not merely an omission — §4 rule 1 (line 103), the §2.1 DoDI 8520.04 and ICAM RD rows (lines 35-36), and the §15 control-mapping row (line 328) all commit to "no self-asserted attributes," yet the GUC seam as specified is precisely a self-assertion channel. §9's failure-mode table (line 242) handles "kernel unreachable" with PEP-side denial and has no row for a compromised PEP, and the defect also falsifies §3.1's guarantee that "compromise of the runtime leaks only its current working set."

findings.relocated_class: Class A relocated: the three-layer split responds to RL#1 B2 (enforcement locus) by moving enforcement into the database, and the database's policy generation/deployment write path — plus the SPIF compiler that feeds all three layers — is now the seam with no trust-plane locus. Same structural shape (a security property asserted over state whose write path is unlocated/unverified), new location. Additionally carries a Class B instance: §6.4 "compiles ... at kernel load" vs §3.9/§6 "trust-plane tooling ... deployed with the migrations" are two representations of where and when the SPIF compile happens, and they disagree.
findings.summary: The RLS generator/migration runner is a third trusted component with no container, no trust classification, no signed output and no DDL credential model; the only assurance is a boot-time parity hash, which cannot detect post-boot policy tampering, cannot compare against SPIF semantics, and presumes a kernel→state-store read path the container architecture never grants.
findings.evidence: 'generated from the SPIF by trust-plane tooling and deployed with the migrations' names a component the trust model does not contain. Boot check 5 compares generator output to deployed policy, so a compromised generator passes. FORCE RLS, BYPASSRLS, deny-all defaults and the policies themselves are mutable DDL: one post-boot ALTER TABLE … NO FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY or DROP POLICY removes the backstop until the next kernel boot. Reading pg_policy to hash deployed policy requires a kernel↔state-store SQL path, but §4 says 'access is SQL through layer-2 PEPs only'.
findings.recommendation: Give the generator and migration runner a place in the trust model, sign their output and verify it before deployment; split DDL/owner credentials (absent at runtime) from non-superuser service roles; replace boot-only parity with continuous verification (event trigger on policy DDL, periodic re-hash, live conformance vectors) and specify the kernel's state-store connection (role, path, read scope) or move the check to a trust-plane tool that has one.
findings.verifier_reasoning: Verified against text, survives refutation attempts. (1) container-architecture.md §2's 9-container inventory has no generator/migration-runner entry and assigns no Trust column to "trust-plane tooling", while §1 principle 1 defines the trusted set by the architecture-defeating criterion — which this component meets. An additional two-representations defect the finding missed strengthens it: abac §6.4 says the SPIF "compiles three ways from one file at kernel load" (compiler inside the kernel, load time) while §3.9/§6 say "generated ... by trust-plane tooling and deployed with the migrations" (outside the kernel, deploy time). Under either reading the deploying write path holding DDL against state-data is unlocated; under the §6.4 reading a single compiler feeds Cedar, PEP predicates AND RLS, so its compromise defeats all three layers — which is why the "RLS is only a backstop, disclosure needs L2+L3 to fail identically" mitigation does not rescue the severity: the independence that makes the backstop meaningful is what a compromised/drifted generator destroys. (2) Boot check 5 ("Generated RLS predicates match deployed database policies (parity hash)") compares generator output to generator-derived deployed state — self-referential, confirmed. Partial mitigation exists (§12 item 3 / container-arch §6 run generated policies against real PostgreSQL with conformance vectors in CI), but §4 makes the SPIF deployment-configurable with no baked-in hierarchy, so CI vectors exercise CI's lattice, not the deployment's — the "cannot compare against SPIF semantics" claim survives for any deployment-specific lattice. (3) Check 5 is the only occurrence; the §9.2 runtime fail-closed matrix has no policy-drift row and its state-store rows presume intact policies. Confirmed boot-only. (4) DDL credential model: §7.3 constrains service roles (non-superuser, no BYPASSRLS) but never separates owner/DDL credentials. Strongest counter-argument: a DDL-capable credential can SELECT the tables directly, so DROP POLICY grants no new read capability — only stealth/persistence. The sub-claim survives narrowly because FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is listed precisely so "the table owner is constrained too": the design deliberately binds the owner with a control the owner can revoke in one statement, with no credential separation and no runtime detection. On its own this sub-item is should-fix, not blocker. (5) container-arch §4 state-data row says "no other container mounts it — access is SQL through layer-2 PEPs only", and abac §3 classes the kernel as PDP only (PEPs enumerated as egress-proxy, data-access layers, skill sandbox). The flat-contradiction reading is arguable (metadata read is not data access; §3.9 gives the store "the structured audit query surface", implying some kernel path), but the load-bearing claim — that no kernel state-store connection (role, path, read scope) is specified anywhere while boot check 5 requires one — is plainly true. Nothing in the corpus addresses the generation/deployment integrity chain elsewhere; ADR-0002's supply-chain row covers Rust build artifacts (Cargo.lock, cargo-audit, distroless), not SQL migration or policy-generation provenance. Not excludable under YAGNI: the corpus specifies RLS plumbing at fine grain (SET LOCAL, FORCE RLS, BYPASSRLS, deny-all, NOT NULL) and boot-time parity, so the generation/deployment path is in-altitude by the document's own standard.

findings.rl1_disposition: new — but causally tied to RL#1 Class B. This is the counterweight/dual class created BY the Class B redesign, not a relocation of it: Class B's structural shape was "N representations that must agree," and single-source generation genuinely removes the N representations at this seam (Class B killed here). What replaces it is the opposite structural shape — one representation governing N enforcement surfaces — whose failure mode is correlated rather than divergent. Note the abac-dcs doc post-dates the RL#1 corpus (5e76b96), so this text was never in RL#1 scope; the finding is new text, new class. Strictness check: not a symptom-fix preserving shape, so 'relocated' would be the wrong label — but the corpus should record that the READ-reality/single-source doctrine has a cost in a defense-in-depth stack, and that cost is unbudgeted here.
findings.relocated_class: two-representations-drift (RL#1 Class B) → common-mode-semantic-failure: the single-source-of-truth redesign trades divergence risk for correlated-failure risk wherever the single source feeds layers whose security value is their independence. Same doctrine, inverted failure mode; needs compiler-level assurance to be a net win in a defense-in-depth argument.
findings.summary: All enforcement layers are compiled from one SPIF by one compiler with one semantic model, so the claim that 'disclosure requires multiple independent layers to fail identically' is false by construction — and shared conformance vectors authored against the same model cannot detect the correlated failure.
findings.evidence: §6.4 sells single-source generation as a virtue ('zero drift by construction'); zero drift is exactly zero independence. An inverted releasability containment, a NULL-array semantic, a missed NOFORN interaction or an ordinal off-by-one is emitted identically into Cedar, the RLS predicates and the validators, and the vectors — authored against the same model — do not contain the case the model gets wrong. §12's 'if the kernel and the database ever disagree, CI fails' is a drift detector, not an independence argument.
findings.recommendation: Either rewrite §1.1/§7.3 to the honest claim (independent against per-surface implementation bugs, correlated against SPIF-compiler semantic bugs) and give the compiler its own assurance (formal spec of dominance, differential testing against an independently authored reference, mutation testing), or buy independence by authoring at least one layer's dominance predicate against an independent spec with parity proving agreement rather than generation guaranteeing it.
findings.verifier_reasoning: CONFIRMED against the text; my refutation attempts failed. (1) Internal contradiction is explicit: §1.1 (line 21) claims "multiple independent, independently tested layers," while §12 (283-291) mandates that every label-touching surface passes the *identical* vectors, and §7.3 (200) actually cites identical-vector testing as evidence FOR independence. Identical vectors are the definition of correlated testing. (2) Non-independence of implementation is stated by the corpus itself, not inferred: §6.4 (156-164) compiles Cedar policies, RLS predicates and label validators from one SPIF file at kernel load; §7.1 (184) compiles the SPIF to Cedar entities; §7.3 (192) generates RLS from the SPIF "never hand-written"; and container-architecture §6 (112) calls the RLS predicates "a fourth projection of the same engine, not a new implementation." The layers are independent in emission substrate (Rust predicate injection vs generated SQL), which does buy real independence against per-surface implementation bugs — exactly the honest claim the finding proposes — but not against a semantic error in the one compiler. (3) The corpus's own drift machinery is not an independence argument: §9.1 item 5 (parity hash) and §12's "if the kernel and the database ever disagree, CI fails" compare two outputs of the same compiler and cannot fire on a uniform error. (4) Attempted refutation via existing assurance: vectors are seeded by harvesting the MCP's ABAC/SPIF suites (285) — genuinely independent provenance — plus proptest properties and mutation testing (293). These are real partial mitigations but do not restore the claim: mutation testing detects tests that fail to kill code mutants, not a specification that is uniformly wrong; the stated properties (reflexive/antisymmetric/transitive dominance, HWM is a lattice join, monotone RLS predicates) are all satisfied by an ordinal off-by-one and by a releasability containment inverted consistently across the model; and an MCP-seeded corpus does not cover the SPIF's new surface (deployment-declared lattices, equivalency maps, handling domains, coalition tetragraphs). (5) No section scopes any assurance for the compiler's semantics — §12, §9.1, §13 (Phase A), §15, §16 (D4/D8/D15) and §17's open questions contain no formal dominance spec, no independently authored reference predicate, and no differential testing. So the recommendation names a real, unfilled gap rather than demanding something the corpus deliberately deferred; nothing in the YAGNI/deny-by-default doctrine excludes an honest scoping of the independence claim (which is a prose fix costing nothing). Severity: retained blocker. The concrete disclosure risk is contingent on a compiler bug, but the defect here is that the document's load-bearing doctrinal claim ("breaches are cut off at the design stage… we do not disclose") is unsound as constructed, and the false assurance actively suppresses the compensating controls a design-stage document is supposed to schedule. In a corpus whose entire thesis is design-stage containment, an unsound defense-in-depth argument is the exact thing to block ratification on; it is ADR-worthy (fits alongside the RL#1 §5 docket, closest to a new ADR on lattice/compiler assurance extending proposed ADR-0008). external_floor is false: this terminates against a patchable seam (formal dominance spec + differential testing against an independently authored reference + at least one layer's predicate authored independently with parity proving rather than generation guaranteeing agreement), not against any invariant outside the system's control.

findings.relocated_class: Class A (enforcement asserted without a trust-plane locus) — NOT relocated and NOT killed for the lake: the abac document builds a genuine three-layer answer for the new state-store container and asserts the multi-layer property corpus-wide, while the lake path is explicitly carried forward "unchanged". The class persists at its original seam (§7.2 / container §6.3), with the added defect that §1 doctrine 1 and §7.3 now overclaim layer-independence for a path that has only one layer.
findings.summary: RL#1 B2 is OPEN: the hook-B non-disclosing disclosure gate may still execute entirely inside the untrusted lake via local maknae-dcs-core bindings chosen 'by measurement', there is no Layer-3 analogue for the corpus, and container §6's 'five of six containers never evaluate policy / parsing is not evaluating' directly contradicts permitting local evaluation there.
findings.evidence: §7.2 marks the choice 'unchanged'; §1 doctrine 1 and §7.3 assert multi-layer independence that does not exist for markdown-on-a-volume. Running the canonical Rust crate does not make the calling container trusted — a compromised lake bypasses the binding or returns unfiltered objects, and no trust-plane verify-on-delivery step was added. This is the store that actually holds the SECRET//REL content of the §8.2 worked flow.
findings.recommendation: Adopt the RL#1 remedy: kernel bulk-decision with verify-on-delivery, or a trusted retrieval broker with lake demoted to a dumb store; if local bindings are retained for throughput, define them as a performance pre-filter the kernel re-verifies before delivery. Publish a per-store enforcement table (Lake vs state store × Layer 1/2/3) and reconcile container §6's parse-vs-evaluate wording with what the lake actually does.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
Verified against the text, not the summary.

(1) The carry-forward is literal. abac-dcs-architecture.md:188 (§7.2) states the lake hot path "uses either a kernel bulk-decision API or local maknae-dcs-core bindings; the choice is made by measurement ... (container-architecture §6, unchanged)." §17 Q2 restates it as a measurement question. RL#1 B2 named exactly this construct (container-arch §3.5/§6.3); the new document re-adopts it verbatim and self-labels it "unchanged". That is a carried-forward blocker, not a resolved one.

(2) The RL#1 remedy is absent. A grep across all three design docs for verify-on-delivery / broker / dumb store / pre-filter / re-verify returns no hits outside container §6.3's own binding sentence. No trust-plane re-verification of lake-returned objects exists anywhere in the corpus. Running the canonical crate inside the untrusted container is a correctness control (no divergence between implementations), not a trust control — a compromised lake calls the binding with a widened subject context, ignores its verdict, or returns objects it never filtered, and nothing downstream notices.

(3) The Layer-3 asymmetry is real. §7.3 defines Layer 3 as PostgreSQL RLS only, and its closing claim — "Disclosure requires Layer 2 and Layer 3 to fail identically" — is scoped to state-store rows. §3.1 line 77 says the Lake is "Unchanged by this document." container-architecture §4 keeps lake-data as lake(rw), dreamer(rw), kernel(label verification, ro) — kernel read-only on labels, with no role on the retrieval path. So for markdown-on-a-volume, Layer 2 IS Layer 1 IS the only layer, and it sits in the untrusted plane. §1 doctrine 1 ("multiple independent, independently tested layers to fail identically") and §8.2's non-disclosing SECRET//REL filtering are asserted globally over a mechanism that exists for one of the two stores. §12's conformance vectors test that the crate is correct; they cannot test that an untrusted caller invoked it honestly.

(4) Materiality: §8.2 is the worked flow where the lake holds the SECRET//REL coalition knowledge and REL-dominance filtering for partner-nation operators is the advertised property. The store with the strongest disclosure requirement has the weakest enforcement locus.

Refutation attempts that failed: OpenTDF (§11) is Phase B and only a *candidate* at-rest format for restricted-category payloads (§17 Q6 open) — not a Layer-3 analogue, and explicitly out of MVP (§13 Phase A). KLC §12's "re-verify signatures before honoring tiers" governs cross-site import, not per-subject retrieval. The §3.1 "runtime plane is stateless" principle routes working sets through the *state store*, not the lake. §9.2's "PEP bug / predicate omission → RLS backstop returns fewer rows" is again state-store-only. Nothing rescues the lake path. A YAGNI/deferral defense also fails: the corpus does not defer the property, it asserts it (§1.1, §8.2) while deferring the mechanism.

One limb of the finding is weaker than stated: container §6.1's "five of six containers never evaluate policy" and §6.2's "parsing is not evaluating" can be read as distinguishing Cedar *policy* evaluation from §6.3's lattice-math/dominance evaluation, so "directly contradicts" overstates it. But that is a wording defense, not a substantive one — a dominance check that determines which objects reach a subject is the disclosure decision whatever it is called, and the §6.1/§6.3 tension is itself a live two-representations seam. The finding survives without this limb.

Severity independently re-assessed as blocker: the defect falsifies a stated doctrine (§1.1) and a worked-flow security claim (§8.2) about the store holding the highest-classification content, and it is the kind of enforcement-locus call that is expensive to unwind after implementation begins (the review's own §5 flags ADR-0004/0005 for exactly this reason). Draft status and the presence of §17 Q2 do not downgrade it, because Q2 poses the question in performance terms and therefore cannot resolve it — the framing is part of the defect.

findings.relocated_class: Class A (enforcement asserted without a trust-plane locus) relocated into the new abac-dcs-architecture.md at the Cedar `context` seam. RL#1 §2 lists among the verifiers' own synonymous phrasings "**PDP decision inputs sourced from less-trusted planes without kernel verification**" — this finding is a literal instance of that phrasing, in a document written after RL#1's scope (`5e76b96`) and after the redesign recommendation. The new document rigorously fixes the class for subject attributes (§5.3 moves attribute binding out of the token entirely; §4 rule 1 Tier-0 store; §7.2 kernel-minted subject context) and for resource labels (§6.4 SPIF, §7.3 RLS), then reintroduces the identical structural shape on the third ABAC input class. Same shape — a trust-plane decision computed over a value the untrusted plane hands it — so this is relocation, not a kill. Direct siblings in the RL#1 blocker docket: B21 (`issuance_type` self-asserted) and B22 (kernel rubber-stamps the dreamer's semantic assertion).
findings.summary: Environment attributes are a first-class Cedar decision input for all six hooks but are 'supplied by the requesting plane and attested where the platform can attest them' — a self-assertion channel the same document forbids for subject attributes, with no stated floor.
findings.evidence: The requesting plane for hooks B, C, E and F is runtime/lake/dreamer, untrusted by design. A compromised runtime asserting network_location: internal, channel_origin: direct-dm or a favourable sandbox_posture gets whatever those attributes buy in policy. 'Attested where the platform can attest them' is precisely the grace mode §1 doctrine 2 says does not exist.
findings.recommendation: Partition environment attributes into kernel-derived (time, channel origin from the gateway's authenticated session record, network location from the kernel's own view), platform-attested (sandbox/host posture), and non-attestable; permit only the first two in Cedar context, make a policy referencing an unattested attribute a boot-time validation failure, and make a missing attested attribute deny. Remove 'supplied by the requesting plane' as a permitted source.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
Verified against the text; I attacked it three ways and it survived.

TEXT (abac-dcs-architecture.md §4, line 99): "**Environment attributes** are the third input class (per SP 800-207 and DoDI 8520.04), named explicitly: time, network location, host/sandbox posture (already an attested policy input at hook F), channel origin. They ride in Cedar's `context`, **supplied by the requesting plane and attested where the platform can attest them**." §7.1 (line 182) then makes context a decision input for ALL six hooks: "All six KLC hooks are Cedar evaluations over (principal…, action, resource = labels, context = environment attributes)."

The internal contradiction is real and same-document:
- §1 doctrine 2: "Absence of a rule, an attribute, a label, a signature, or a reachable decision point is a denial. There is no grace mode." "Attested where the platform can attest them" is definitionally a grace mode for the residue.
- §2.1 states the constraint unconditionally, not scoped to subjects: DoDI 8520.04 row — "attributes only from authoritative attribute services (§3.4, §4.3)… self-asserted claims are never an attribute source"; ICAM RD row — "self-asserted attributes are low-assurance… no self-assertion". §4 rule 1 then repeats "No self-asserted attributes" for subject attributes while the sentence four lines above blesses exactly that channel for environment attributes.
- The requesting planes for hooks B/C/E/F are `runtime`, `lake`, `dreamer`, all "Untrusted by design" (container-architecture.md §2, lines 25–27).

Refutation attempts that failed:
1. "The corpus fixes it elsewhere." It does not. §9.1's seven boot-blocking checks cover SPIF, authority map, attribute store, Cedar schema+vectors, RLS parity, FIPS, instance ceiling — nothing constrains which context attributes a policy may reference or requires them attestable. §9.2's fail-closed matrix enumerates eight failure rows (kernel unreachable, drift, missing labels, unlabeled row, PEP bug, egress failure, Vault sealed, uncertified category) and has **no row for a missing/forged/unattested environment attribute** — the one enumeration where it would have to appear if it were handled. §7.2's kernel-minted subject context covers *subject* attributes only.
2. "Layer 2/3 backstop it." RLS predicates are generated from the SPIF over classification/releasability/subject/handling (§7.3) — they carry no environment dimension, so a context-conditioned permit has no at-rest backstop. This is the one place the three-layer defence genuinely has a single layer.
3. "It's YAGNI / no policy uses it yet." §7.1 makes context a first-class input to every hook, and §2.1 claims DoDI 8520.04 conformance *on the strength of* environment attributes. You cannot both cite them as the conformance basis and treat their trust source as out of scope.

Partial correction to the finding's detail, recorded for honesty: `sandbox_posture` is the *weakest* of its three examples — §4 parenthesises it as "already an attested policy input at hook F" and KLC line 213 says "Sandbox strength is a declared, attested host property." That instance is arguably covered. `network_location`, `channel_origin`, and `time` carry the defect with no stated source, and "supplied by the requesting plane" stands unqualified as a permitted source for all of them. The finding is confirmed on those three, not on sandbox posture.

External floor: no. Every remedy the recommendation names is inside the system's own control — the gateway already holds an authenticated session record (§5.2/§5.3) from which channel origin and network location are kernel-derivable, and §9.1 is an existing boot-validation seam where an "only attestable attributes in context" check drops in. Nothing here terminates against an invariant outside the design.

findings.section: §7.1 ('all six KLC hooks are Cedar evaluations') vs KLC §10 hook D and §9.1

The visible relocation marker is §4 L99's "supplied by the requesting plane and attested where the platform can attest them" - context attributes are conceded to be requester-supplied with attestation left conditional. findings.summary: RL#1 B22 is RELOCATED and formalized: hook D's semantic promotion criteria (dedup complete, corroborating sources independent, N supervised executions) are not Cedar-checkable, so they arrive as attributes computed by the untrusted dreamer — the rubber stamp now wearing a deny-by-default wrapper.
findings.evidence: Cedar evaluates supplied attributes; it cannot determine whether dedup was complete or two sources genuinely independent. No attestation model was added anywhere in the redesign, and §7.1 draws no distinction between kernel-derived and requester-supplied Cedar inputs. The dreamer remains 'Untrusted by design' and still owns promotion proposals.
findings.recommendation: Partition every §9 criterion into kernel-verifiable (signature presence, tier arithmetic, ceiling bounds, execution counts from the kernel's own audit log) and dreamer-attested (semantic agreement, dedup, corroboration independence); require attested claims to carry kernel-checkable evidence (corroboration names object ids so issuer-distinctness and lineage-disjointness are mechanically verified); require operator sign-off for attestation-only Tier-1 promotions; state in §7.1 that Cedar context may hold only kernel-derived or attested-and-verified attributes.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
Verified against the text, and survived four refutation attempts.

EVIDENCE FOR THE DEFECT
- abac-dcs-architecture.md §7.1 (L182): "All six KLC hooks are Cedar evaluations over (principal = operator or task identity, action, resource = labels, context = environment attributes) ... Deny by default; forbid overrides permit." No distinction anywhere between kernel-derived and requester-supplied Cedar inputs.
- KLC §10 hook D (L209) is unchanged from RL#1: "Criteria of §9 met; one tier per gate; signature requirements; audit before/after."
- KLC §9.1 (L184-185) criteria are semantic and not mechanically checkable: "dedup complete"; "Corroborated by a second independent ceiling-1 source (independence definition: §14 Q8)"; "Confirmed across >=3 independent sessions". §14 Q8 (L265) remains "Operator: undecided as of 2026-07-14" - so §9.1 cites an undefined definition.
- container-architecture.md inventory row 6 and §3.6 (L58): `dreamer` is still "Untrusted by design" and still owns "promotion *proposals*".
- No attestation model was added: the only attestation language in the ABAC doc is §4 L99 ("Environment attributes ... ride in Cedar's context, supplied by the requesting plane and attested where the platform can attest them") and the hook-F sandbox-posture reference. L99 is corroborating evidence for the finding, not a rebuttal - it concedes requester-supplied context and makes attestation conditional/optional.
- Decision log §16 (D1-D17) and open questions §17 contain no attestation decision or open item. No ADR-0005/0011 exists in the repo (ADR-0001/0002/0003 only), so RL#1's recommendation is unlanded.

REFUTATIONS ATTEMPTED AND FAILED
1. "Cedar can evaluate it, so §7.1 is not false." Formally true - Cedar can evaluate `dedup_complete == true`. That IS the laundering: deny-by-default machinery applied over an attacker-supplied premise yields a decided, not verified, outcome. The §7.1 sentence is technically true and materially misleading; the doc draws no provenance distinction that would let an implementer notice.
2. "Fail-closed doctrine §1.2 covers it." Absence of an attribute is a denial; a supplied-true attribute is not absent.
3. "No self-asserted attributes" (§2.1 L35, §4 rule 1 L103, §5.2 item 3 L131, D7). Every one of these is scoped to SUBJECT attributes bound from the Tier-0 signed store. None governs resource or context attributes entering the Cedar context. The §3 PIP row ("lake stamps labels at ingest as directed by kernel decisions") does not close the loop, because the kernel's hook-D direction is itself conditioned on the dreamer's semantic claim.
4. "Tier-1 promotions require signatures (KLC §8 step 5; §6 L90 'operator or CI key')." Partial and ambiguous mitigation only: a CI key signs whatever the pipeline computed and attests nothing semantic; RL#1 B7 already flags the signed payload as undefined over mutable frontmatter; and the §9.1 document 2->1 gate is corroboration OR operator sign-off, so the corroboration path needs no human. Narrows blast radius; does not refute.

SEVERITY: blocker sustained. Tier 1 is "the official way to do things" and the executable tier for signed skills; an untrusted-plane-controlled path into it is the exact single-compromised-source poisoning path KLC §11.2 claims to close.

SHARPENING FOR THE HAND-OFF (strengthens the recommendation): more of §9 is kernel-derivable than the finding assumes. The kernel is the append-only audit writer and owns hook F (container-arch §3.1), so "N successful supervised executions with zero policy denials" is countable from kernel-held state, as are tier arithmetic, ceiling bounds, signature presence, and hash verification. Corroboration independence becomes mechanically checkable if the claim must name corroborating object IDs (issuer-distinctness and lineage-disjointness are kernel-visible). The residual attestation surface is narrow (content agreement, dedup completeness) - which is why operator sign-off for attestation-only Tier-1 promotions is a proportionate fallback, not a heavy one.
