findings.verifier_reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not on the core claim.

Direct text comparison:
- `design/container-architecture.md` §6 item 2 (line 107): "**Representation is schema-first.** The `dcs_label` block and the kernel decision request/response protocol are versioned schemas (JSON Schema at MVP); per-language types are generated, never hand-rolled." Under this, JSON Schema is the generative root and *per-language types* — which includes `maknae-dcs-core`'s Rust label types — are outputs. Item 3 (line 108) names `maknae-dcs-core` "the single canonical implementation" of *label types, lattice math, dominance checks*, i.e. canonical for **evaluation**, sitting alongside (not above) the schema-first representation rule.
- `design/abac-dcs-architecture.md` §6.2 (line 144): "Same vocabulary, same lattice, both projections generated from `maknae-dcs-core`'s types (container-architecture §6: schema-first; per-language types generated, never hand-rolled)." This makes the Rust types the root from which the YAML frontmatter schema and the DCS columns derive — and cites container §6 as the authority for it, when container §6's sentence says the opposite direction (types are the generated thing). §6.2 is also enshrined as decision D8 (line 354: "generated from `maknae-dcs-core` types"), so the inversion is carried into the decision register, not just prose.

The charitable reading — "types are themselves schema-generated, so 'from the types' is transitively schema-first" — is available but is exactly the ambiguity being flagged: it leaves undetermined which artifact is checked in and which is regenerated, and the inline citation asserts agreement that the cited sentence does not supply. That is the corpus's own Class B pattern (two statements of one fact that must stay in sync) applied to the generative root itself.

Partial refutation of the finding's secondary claim: it is not true that *neither* document names a mechanism for any projection. For the **RLS/columns** side the corpus is specific — container line 112: RLS predicates "generated from the SPIF by trust-plane tooling (never hand-written SQL), parity-checked at kernel boot, and run against the identical conformance vectors on a real PostgreSQL in CI"; abac §7.3 (line 192) and §12 (lines 287–293) corroborate, including property tests that generated RLS predicates are monotone. So there is a named drift backstop for the RLS projection. What genuinely has **no** named generator, build step, or regeneration-diff CI gate is the label-representation chain itself: JSON Schema → per-language types → YAML frontmatter schema (KLC §6). Conformance vectors catch *behavioral* divergence, not *representation* divergence (a frontmatter key present in the schema but absent from the Rust type, or vice versa, is not something a lattice-dominance vector exercises). Note also abac §6.4 introduces the SPIF as "one vocabulary source" compiling three ways — I checked whether that is a third competing root and concluded it is not: SPIF governs the lattice declaration (levels/categories/communities), a different axis from label field representation. No conflict there, but it does mean the corpus already has one artifact with an explicit "compiles N ways from one file" statement, which is the shape §6.2 should have been given.

No external fact is needed to settle this; it is a text-vs-text contradiction inside the repo.

findings.relocated_class: Class A — enforcement asserted without a trust-plane locus; the three-layer redesign killed it on the read/disclosure half and relocated it to the derivation/write-and-label-stamping half (adjacent to open B10/B11/B12)
findings.summary: 'RLS failure mode is always fewer rows' is true only for SELECT under a correct predicate: a dominance predicate cannot prevent write-down on UPDATE, NOT NULL cannot prevent a wrong label on INSERT, and a permissive generated predicate yields more rows, not fewer — so the derivation/label-stamping path has no Layer-3 backstop at all.
findings.evidence: A subject cleared to SECRET satisfies dominance for every row at or below SECRET, so an UPDATE rewriting classification from secret to unclass passes both USING and any WITH CHECK derived from the same relation — the exact act KLC §15 declares classification_downgrade_by_automation: never. A PEP that fails to join the high-water mark and inserts classification='unclass' on a row assembled from SECRET inputs produces a NOT NULL row that passes deny-all defaults and dominance and is thereafter invisible to no one. Permissive USING on DELETE/UPDATE is an integrity/availability failure the phrase does not cover.
findings.recommendation: Give the write path its own Layer-3 controls: generated WITH CHECK policies pinning label columns against downgrade (decrease only via a distinct role or a consumed signed-downgrade authorization), database-side constraints/triggers re-verifying the high-water relation for lineage-bearing rows, subject-ownership checks on INSERT; amend the §9.2 PEP-bug row to cover label-stamping bugs; add a row for a permissive generated predicate; soften the 'always fewer rows' claim.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
I tried to refute this three ways and it survived all three.

**1. Is the §7.3 sentence misread?** No. `design/abac-dcs-architecture.md:200` reads verbatim: "RLS failure mode is always *fewer* rows. Disclosure requires Layer 2 and Layer 3 to fail identically." The second sentence scopes to *disclosure*, which is the strongest refutation available — but it does not rescue the claim, because the surrounding text makes the coverage claim unqualified in three other places: §7 (`:178`) "decision, enforcement, and at-rest layers, **each of which independently denies**"; §9.2 (`:246`) "PEP bug / predicate omission | RLS backstop returns fewer rows; single-layer failure discloses nothing" — a row the doc itself calls "a testable acceptance criterion (§12)"; and §15 (`:330`) "Bell-LaPadula dominance **at three layers**; no automated downgrade | AC-3(3), AC-4, AC-16(6)" — an assessor-facing control claim. A label-stamping PEP bug is a PEP bug; the matrix row asserts a backstop that does not exist for it.

**2. Is the write path covered elsewhere in the corpus?** Partially, and not at Layer 3. §6.4 item 3 (`:162`) compiles the SPIF into "Label validators (ingest and write-path schema enforcement)" — a real mitigation the finding does not mention, so the phrase "no Layer-3 backstop **at all**" is fair but "no write-path control at all" would not be. However those validators enforce vocabulary/schema well-formedness, not that a derived row's label equals the high-water mark of its lineage, and the doc assigns them no plane/locus. The five §7.3 bullets are exhaustively read-side or absence-side: `SET LOCAL` GUCs, `FORCE RLS`, no `BYPASSRLS`, deny-all default, `NOT NULL` labels. `NOT NULL` makes an *unlabeled* row unrepresentable (§9.2 `:245` claims exactly and only that); it says nothing about a *wrong* label. I grepped the whole document for `WITH CHECK`, trigger, constraint, generated column, INSERT/UPDATE policy — zero hits. §12's RLS vector (`:289`) is "insert labeled rows, set subject GUCs, assert exact row visibility": read-visibility only, so the write direction is also unexercised by the conformance spine.

**3. Are the PostgreSQL mechanics as claimed?** Yes, and this is the load-bearing part. The generated predicate is described (`:192`) as "dominance predicate over the classification ordinal + releasability array containment + `noforn` + `subject`/`handling_grants` join" — a pure subject-dominates-row test. Under Postgres semantics a `FOR ALL` policy's USING expression is also applied as the WITH CHECK for INSERT/UPDATE unless a distinct WITH CHECK is given, so a SECRET-cleared subject satisfies it for every row at or below SECRET. An UPDATE rewriting `classification` secret→unclass passes both the old-row USING and the new-row check; an INSERT stamping `unclass` on a row assembled from SECRET inputs passes deny-all, dominance and NOT NULL. That is `classification_downgrade_by_automation: never` (KLC `:286`) and "No automated downgrade, ever" (abac `:260`) with no at-rest mechanism behind it. The finding's third sub-claim also holds: an over-permissive *generated* predicate yields more rows, not fewer — and §9.1's parity-hash check (`:170`-block item 5) only detects drift between generated and deployed policy, not a wrong generator, while §6.4's one-file-three-surfaces compilation makes a SPIF-compilation bug a **common-mode** failure across all three layers, directly undercutting "implemented independently" at `:200`.

Nothing in the YAGNI/deny-by-default doctrine excludes the recommendation — WITH CHECK policies pinning label columns against decrease, and a lineage/HWM re-verification trigger, are the same "make it unrepresentable at the type level" move the doc already makes with `NOT NULL`, applied to the value rather than its presence.

**Severity, reassessed down from blocker to should-fix.** Layers 1 and 2 do nominally cover the write path (hook C HWM derivation is a Cedar evaluation; §6.4 write-path validators exist), so this is not a total bypass of the labeling model the way RL#1's B1 (untrusted `rw` on the frontmatter that *is* the tier state) was. What is verified is (i) a genuine defense-in-depth asymmetry — the at-rest layer is read-only in coverage while the document claims three-layer independence — and (ii) two false statements in artifacts meant to be consumed as truth: a §9.2 row labeled a testable acceptance criterion, and a §15 control-mapping row an assessor would read as "downgrade prevented at three layers." (ii) is the sharpest part and is the reason this stays above discussion.

**Relocation, not new.** I disagree with the submitted `rl1_disposition: new`. The doc is outside RL#1's stated scope (`:8`), so "new document" is true, but the *defect shape* is RL#1 Class A — "the contract repeatedly names a security property but the mechanism that would enforce it either lives in the untrusted plane or is not specified" (`:20`). The three-layer architecture is the redesign answering ADR-0005 (enforcement locus). It killed the class on the **disclosure/read** half — that half now has a named, independent at-rest locus. It left the **derivation/write** half exactly where RL#1 found it: a "never" invariant (KLC §15, echoed at abac `:260` and `:330`) asserted with the enforcing mechanism unnamed at the layer the document credits for it. Same structural shape, new seam — relocated. It also leaves RL#1's B10/B11/B12 (write-down via HWM, no-write-down on replies, no component mints labels) untouched at the at-rest layer.

findings.summary: The certification gate lets operator-declared but uncertified restricted-category data (PHI/PII/GDPR) be ingested and processed with only a warning — verbatim the 'starting with warnings' §1.2 prohibits — unbounded in time, with no capability reduction and no signed risk acceptance.
findings.evidence: §9.2 codifies it as intended runtime behavior. A warning is not a control: the absent thing is an accreditation artifact, and §1.2's list of absences-that-deny does not exempt it. 'Loud until certified' permits 'forever, uncertified'; the uncertified state does not restrict egress, so the data can still be assembled into context and routed at hook E to a remote endpoint — the highest-consequence path. §6.5 option 3 already establishes the stronger artifact (a Tier-0 certification reference) but does not require anything signed for the risky path, so §15's PL-2 mapping overstates it.
findings.recommendation: Require a Tier-0 operator-signed acceptance-of-risk artifact with an expiry before any uncertified restricted-category processing (absence then denies and §1.2 holds unmodified), and force no-egress or locally-accredited-endpoint-only while uncertified. If warn-only is genuinely intended, amend §1.2 to name the certification gate as the single enumerated exception with its reasoning recorded.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
I tried to refute this and the narrow core survives, but three of its escalating claims do not — which is why the blocker framing fails.

WHAT IS TEXTUALLY TRUE (verified):
- §1.2 reads verbatim: "Fail closed, everywhere. Absence of a rule, an attribute, a label, a signature, or a reachable decision point is a denial. There is no grace mode, no cached-allow, no 'starting with warnings.'"
- §6.5 option 2 reads: "Operator-declared but uncertified → ingest and processing proceed, and every touch of that data stamps a persistent, un-silenceable 'NOT CERTIFIED for [category]' warning... Conscious opt-in, loud until certified."
- §9.2's last row codifies it as intended runtime behavior: "Uncertified-category data touched | Operation proceeds (category was operator-declared)..."
- §16 D3 ratifies it. Nowhere in the three design docs is there an expiry, a time bound, a review cadence, or any signed acceptance-of-risk artifact for the uncertified state. `grep` for expiry/acceptance across the corpus returns nothing. So "loud until certified" does permit "loud forever, uncertified," and §1.2 is stated as unconditional doctrine with no enumerated exception pointing at §6.5. That is a real doctrine-vs-mechanism seam and it is patchable in one paragraph.

WHAT I REFUTE IN THE FINDING:
1. "No capability reduction... the data can still be assembled into context and routed at hook E to a remote endpoint — the highest-consequence path." This misreads the corpus. Hook E is not certification-blind: KLC §6 requires the *endpoint's operator-signed accredited label to dominate the payload's high-water mark*, and the SPIF (§6.4) explicitly includes "handling domains" in the compiled vocabulary. §8.1's worked flow states it directly — "health-labeled context routes only to endpoints the operator's deployment authorized for health data" — and §6.3 puts `no-egress`/`operator-only` caveats at hooks B/E. So uncertified restricted-category data is *already* capability-reduced on the egress path by an operator-signed artifact (the endpoint registration, whose signature is a §9.1 boot precondition). The claim that nothing signed guards the risky path is false; the correct, weaker claim is that the signed artifact guarding it is an endpoint accreditation rather than a category certification.
2. "'Starting with warnings' — verbatim what §1.2 prohibits." The phrase is doing weaker work than the finding assumes. Read in situ alongside §9.1 ("The kernel refuses to start on invalid security configuration... no degraded mode"), "starting with warnings" most naturally denotes *system startup in a degraded mode*, not per-object processing. The clash is real but is a wording/carve-out defect, not a verbatim self-contradiction.
3. "§1.2's list of absences-that-deny does not exempt it." §1.2's list is an enumeration — rule, attribute, label, signature, reachable decision point. A missing *accreditation artifact* is none of those; and the data in question is fully labeled, fully attributed, and fully decided at every hook. The certification gate withholds a compliance attestation, not an access control. The finding treats an enumerated list as if it were open-ended.
4. "§15's PL-2 mapping overstates it." Weakest limb. The row reads "CM-3, PL-2 (documented deviation with visibility)"; the gate produces un-silenceable log/UI/audit stamps plus a Tier-0 config state — that is literally visibility, and §15 is labeled "(informative)" with "Full matrix belongs in the RMF package." The "documented" half is thin without a signed artifact, which is a fair nit, not evidence of a blocker.

RESIDUE THAT JUSTIFIES ACTION: the unbounded duration of the uncertified state (no expiry, no re-review, no signed acceptance) and §1.2 asserting an unconditional rule that §6.5/§9.2/D3 knowingly except. The finding's recommendation is directionally right but over-scoped: forcing "no-egress or locally-accredited-endpoint-only while uncertified" partly duplicates a control the corpus already has at hook E. The minimal correct fix is (a) bound the uncertified state with a Tier-0 operator-signed acceptance carrying an expiry, and (b) amend §1.2 to name the certification gate as the single enumerated exception with its reasoning — which also feeds RL#1's still-open "accepted-residuals register" gap (#41 / new-doc 0012).

Severity: should-fix, not blocker. No enforcement layer is disabled, no unlabeled data exists, the egress path retains an independent signed control, and the behavior is a ratified deliberate decision (D3) in a document whose Status is "Draft — rough architecture for team review." A blocker in this corpus is a mechanism that discloses; this one is an accreditation-governance gap plus a doctrine-text carve-out that was never written down.

findings.evidence: The origin schema tolerated this because determination was a human, guide-driven act (the source is explicit that its analogous determinations are OCA decisions and phases the privacy apparatus to 'Phase D — when PII enters the system'), whereas Maknae's flagship MVP flow puts PHI into the state store in Phase A. findings.verifier_reasoning:
Verified against the text, with one sub-claim struck.

CONFIRMED (core): §6.5's three states key entirely on the *presence* of an operator declaration. Step 1 is "Undeclared category → ingest refused (hook A dominance check against the instance ceiling)"; step 2 is "Operator-declared but uncertified." §9.2's matrix row makes the trigger explicit — "Uncertified-category data touched | Operation proceeds (category was operator-declared)…". Nothing in §6.4 (label validators enforce *vocabulary* and schema), KLC §6/§10 hook A (dominance vs. the instance ceiling), or KLC §12 (import re-verifies signatures + ceiling dominance) tests whether a declared label is *true*. So health data ingested under a non-restricted label passes every gate silently, and the loud NOT-CERTIFIED apparatus never fires. Meanwhile §4 rule 1 and the §15 control row ("Subject attributes from authoritative signed store; no self-assertion | IA-2, AC-16") make no-self-assertion a load-bearing rule for subjects, and no counterpart rule or minting authority exists for resource labels/categories. That asymmetry is real and undocumented — §17's seven open questions do not include it, and there is no residual register anywhere in the corpus (RL#1 #41/#66/#68 flagged the absence; ADR-0012 is proposed but unwritten). The contract-honesty defect stands: an implementer reading §6.5 + §15 (which maps the gate to PT-2, a privacy-authority control) can reasonably read the gate as a privacy-compliance control when it is only an operator-visibility control over *declared* categories.

REFUTED (sub-claim): "Reconcile 'deferred from MVP' with §8.1 making PHI a Phase-A workload" misreads §6.5. What is deferred is *certifications*, not PHI handling — "The base deployment ships with zero certified restricted categories… deferred from MVP as certifications, present from birth as schema," and §13 Phase A explicitly lists "certification gate warning loudly." §8.1's health flow at Phase A is exactly the intended state-2 behavior (declared, uncertified, loud). There is no contradiction there, and that half of the recommendation should be dropped.

PARTIALLY DISCOUNTED (remedy): the "kernel-side detection path (classifier/heuristic flagging at ingest)" half is doctrinally disfavored here — a content classifier is a *reconstruction* of ground truth (the RL doctrine's READ-reality heuristic, and the corpus's own YAGNI/deny-by-default posture), and it would import false-positive cost into a fail-closed ingest path. The surviving actionable remedy is documentation-shaped: state plainly in §6.5 that the gate is a visibility control over declared categories (not detection or compliance), add the resource-label counterpart to §4 rule 1 (who is authorized to mint/declare a category, and that the kernel binds nothing about label truth), and carry undetected-misdeclaration as a named residual (§9.2 or the ADR-0012 residual register). A provenance-bound path — labels inherited from an authoritative labeled source rather than authored at ingest — is the only structural mitigation worth naming.

Severity: should-fix, not blocker. Nothing is bypassed that a truthful declaration would have caught; the defect is an unstated limitation on a control the document elsewhere maps to a privacy control family, plus an unrecorded residual. It is not merely "discussion" because the remedy is concrete and the §4/§6.5 asymmetry actively misleads.

findings.summary: The flagship worked flow processes exactly the data class §6.5 names as the gate's first user, in a deployment that ships with zero certified categories, yet never mentions the gate, the NOT-CERTIFIED warning, a write, a Layer-2/Layer-3 disagreement, or an audited denial.
findings.evidence: §12 promotes the §8 flows to end-to-end acceptance tests, so the omission propagates into the suite: the 'every touch' requirement gets no coverage from the one flow that would exercise it. The flow also treats health purely as a handling value while §6.5 speaks of restricted categories, and the document never says whether those are one axis or two.
findings.recommendation: State the deployment's certification posture in §8.1 and show the gate firing (or the Tier-0 certification reference silencing it); clarify whether restricted categories and handling domains are one axis; add the write leg (session row born at the HWM, INSERT passing WITH CHECK) and one denial leg with its audit event.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
Core defect verified against the text, but with roughly half the stated evidence refuted, so the finding survives on a narrower and different basis than as written.

WHAT HOLDS:
(1) §6.5 (line 174): "The base deployment ships with zero certified restricted categories. GDPR/PII/PHI regimes are the expected first users of this gate." §16 D13 (line 359) explicitly types the §8.1 flow as "health assistant (PHI-class)". The flagship worked flow is therefore processing exactly the data class the gate names as its first user, in a posture the document says ships zero-certified.
(2) §8.1 (line 206) narrates auth -> attribute bind -> hook B -> RLS -> HWM context -> hook E routing -> egress-proxy -> "audit events at every hop", and never mentions the certification gate, the deployment's certification posture, or the un-silenceable "NOT CERTIFIED for [category]" stamp that §6.5 case 2 requires on EVERY touch. Confirmed by direct read.
(3) The axis ambiguity is real and is the load-bearing half. §6.4 (line 158) enumerates the SPIF as "levels, category sets, releasability communities, handling domains, equivalency maps" — categories and handling domains as separate elements — while §4 (line 94) has `handling_grants: [health-self, finance-self]  # civilian regimes` and §6.5 frames the gate over restricted categories whose first users are PHI/PII/GDPR regimes. Nothing in the corpus states whether the `health` handling domain IS a PHI restricted category. That is not cosmetic: if it is, §8.1 as written is either impossible (§6.5 case 1: undeclared -> ingest refused) or must be loud (case 2); if it is not, the gate's named first user appears in no worked flow at all. The document does not say which.

WHAT I REFUTE:
(a) "never mentions ... an audited denial" — §8.1's closing sentence IS a negative-access leg ("A second operator ... retrieves *nothing* — non-disclosing filtering"), and §12 (line 295) names "cross-subject health query" among the §8 flows' adversarial variants. Overstated.
(b) "the 'every touch' requirement gets no coverage" — §9.2 (line 249) carries the row "Uncertified-category data touched | Operation proceeds ... with the un-silenceable NOT-CERTIFIED warning (§6.5)", and §12 states "every row of the §9.2 matrix becomes a test". The control IS covered by the §12-promoted suite; only the flagship narrative omits it. The propagation-into-the-suite argument, which is the finding's stated reason for severity, therefore largely fails.
(c) "never mentions ... a write" — §8.1 does narrate write-side labeling ("context assembles, labeled at the high-water mark of its inputs"), matching §6.3's HWM birth rule and hook C. The recommendation's INSERT/WITH CHECK ask is a genuinely separate and larger gap (grep confirms "WITH CHECK" appears nowhere in the corpus; §7.3's RLS plumbing list is read-side only) and should be filed on its own, not folded into this one.
(d) "a Layer-2/Layer-3 disagreement" leg — §7.3 and §12 specify that seam mechanically ("If the kernel and the database ever disagree about who sees a row, CI fails before a human could"). Demanding a worked-flow dramatization of it is polish, not a defect.

Net: confirmed as an unresolved label-model question (handling domain vs restricted category — one axis or two?) that manifests as the flagship flow being silent on its own certification posture. Not confirmed as a test-coverage hole. Severity held at should-fix on the strength of the axis ambiguity alone; the "worked example does not exercise its control" half is discussion-tier on its own.

findings.rl1_disposition: open — bears on RL#1 #41 (missing fail-closed / startup-precondition semantics) and its ADR-0012 docket entry (failure-mode & threat-model register). §9.1 substantively answers the startup-precondition half; the runtime register in §9.2 remains incomplete, so #41 is partially addressed but not closed. Not "new," and not relocated: the response is an incomplete answer in the same structural place, not a symptom-fix that moved the class to a new seam.
findings.summary: The matrix omits the failure modes the redesign itself created or made load-bearing — state-store loss or wrong-schema, absent/malformed/replayed GUCs, subject-context signature/audience/key-revocation/clock failures, post-boot RLS DDL tampering, SPIF reload or migration failure, audit-write failure, Cedar evaluation error/timeout, and partial transactions — so 'fail closed, everywhere' is unsubstantiated and each missing row is also a missing test.
findings.evidence: §9.2 declares each row a testable acceptance criterion and §12 confirms every row becomes a test. Under §1.2 the only consistent answer for audit-write failure is that an unauditable operation must be denied, but that availability commitment is nowhere stated, so the default outcome is a silent unaudited allow. §7.1's 'deny by default' covers no-matching-policy, not evaluation errors.
findings.recommendation: Add rows with named mechanisms and observable criteria for: state-store unreachable or schema-parity failure; GUC absence/spoofing; subject-context cryptographic and clock failures; runtime RLS policy divergence; SPIF/migration/parity failure; audit-write failure (deny and halt the affected path); Cedar evaluation error/timeout/indeterminate (deny, audited as an evaluation fault). Confirm §12 picks them up.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
Verified against the text; the core claim holds, though the finding is over-inclusive on three sub-items.

CONFIRMED against the document:
- §9.2 contains exactly 8 rows (kernel unreachable; attribute/registration drift at fire time; missing labels at ingest; unlabeled state-store row; PEP bug/predicate omission; egress-proxy policy failure; Vault sealed; uncertified category). §12 does state "every row of the §9.2 matrix becomes a test," and §9.2 itself says "Each row is a testable acceptance criterion (§12)" — so the register's completeness is directly load-bearing on what gets built and tested.
- **Audit-write failure is genuinely nowhere in the corpus.** §10 asserts kernel-owned append-only audit and "audit events at every hop" (§8.1) but never states what happens when the write fails. §15's control map lists AU-2/3/9/10 and PT-2 — **AU-5 (response to audit processing failures) is absent**. Doctrine §1.2 ("absence of a rule, an attribute, a label, a signature, or a reachable decision point is a denial") does not reach audit: audit is not a decision point, so the doctrine clause cannot be cited as covering it. The default outcome really is an unaudited allow. This is the strongest element.
- **Cedar evaluation error/timeout/indeterminate:** §7.1 says only "Deny by default; forbid overrides permit," which is the no-matching-policy case, exactly as the finding states. Nothing addresses evaluator error or latency bound. Non-trivial in Cedar specifically, where erroring policies are skipped — skipping a *forbid* is not a fail-closed outcome.
- **Post-boot RLS divergence:** §9.1 item 5 checks generated-vs-deployed policy parity **at boot only** ("parity hash — drift is a boot failure"). §7.3's mitigations (FORCE RLS, no BYPASSRLS, non-superuser service roles) constrain DML, not DDL by a privileged role. Runtime divergence has no stated detection, and no §9.2 row.
- **GUC absence/spoofing:** §7.3 has attributes arriving as `SET LOCAL` GUCs with no signature verification at the database layer, while §7.2 says the subject context is *signed*. The signature is therefore not checked by Layer 3. This matters more than the finding claims: §7.3/§9.2 assert "disclosure requires Layer 2 and Layer 3 to fail identically," but a compromised or buggy PEP that sets attacker-chosen GUCs defeats both layers with one action, because Layer 3's inputs are supplied by Layer 2. The missing row is real, and the independence claim it undercuts is stronger than an omitted-row framing suggests.
- **Subject-context clock/revocation:** §7.2 covers absent/expired only. Key revocation and clock skew are unstated — though §17 Q4 legitimately defers the envelope format, which softens this to a deferred-by-design item rather than an omission.

PARTIALLY REFUTED (finding is over-inclusive here):
- **SPIF "reload" failure** — no reload path exists in the design; the SPIF "compiles three ways from one file at kernel load" (§6.4) and §9.1 is the boot gate. A restart re-runs boot validation. Not a defect absent a hot-reload feature.
- **Migration failure / schema parity** — §9.1 item 5 plus `NOT NULL` labels and deny-all default policy (§7.3) already make a post-migration mismatch a boot failure or a zero-row table. Residual is only the runtime-DDL case already counted above.
- **Partial transactions** — PostgreSQL transaction atomicity plus transaction-scoped `SET LOCAL` covers this; no argued failure path.
- **State-store unreachable** — a connection failure surfaces as an error, not an allow; the omission is a missing test row, not a live fail-open.

SEVERITY (revised down from blocker to should-fix): the document is explicitly "Draft — rough architecture for team review," and §14 states the rough design binds to no unread details with a final-design re-walk. Nothing in §9.2 is *wrong*; the remedy is additive rows plus their §12 vectors, not a redesign, and the fixes are cheap now and cheaper than after implementation. RL#1 itself classified the analogous gap (#41, missing fail-closed/startup-precondition semantics) as its highest-value **should-fix** with ADR-0012 as the home — consistency argues for the same weight here. Note for the orchestrator: the GUC-supplied-by-Layer-2 issue undercuts the layer-independence claim and is blocker-grade **as its own finding**; it should not be buried as one more row in this register finding.

DRIFT CAUTION (not a refutation): a hand-maintained failure-mode matrix is itself a second representation of the real failure surface and will drift as the design grows — the corpus's own READ-reality doctrine. The remedy should tie rows to mechanisms and conformance vectors (§12) so an untested row fails CI, rather than becoming a prose list that silently falls behind.

findings.summary: Subject-context TTL, task fire-time re-evaluation, token expiry and KLC freshness are all time-dependent, but no trusted time source is named, no clock sanity is boot-checked, and no failure mode covers skew — so a component with a slow clock treats expired contexts as live, the one control bounding the cached-allow window.
findings.evidence: Every expiry comparison is made by the component holding the artifact, not by the kernel. §9.1's seven boot checks say nothing about time and §9.2 has no clock row. The air-gapped deployments §8.2 and KLC §12 contemplate are exactly where time sync is least reliable. Every other control degrades toward denial when a component misbehaves; clock skew degrades toward permission.
findings.recommendation: Mint subject contexts with a kernel-issued monotonic epoch in addition to a wall-clock expiry so a superseded-epoch context is rejected regardless of the PEP's clock; add a §9.1 clock-sanity check and a §9.2 skew row; state the time-sync requirement for the air-gapped profile.
findings.verifier_reasoning: Verified directly against the text. (1) Absence claim is literally true: no occurrence of clock/NTP/skew/monotonic/time-sync anywhere in abac-dcs-architecture.md, container-architecture.md, or knowledge-lifecycle-contract.md; §9.1's seven boot checks and §9.2's eight-row matrix have no time row. (2) §9.2 row 1 confirms the mechanism: "Kernel unreachable | Every PEP denies. No cached-allow; a subject context past TTL is a denial" — the sole control converting kernel-unreachable into denial is a TTL comparison performed by the PEP against its own clock, so a lagging/stopped clock silently turns no-cached-allow into cached-allow. Uniquely among the matrix rows, the failure direction is toward permission. (3) The finding under-cites its strongest evidence: §4 names "time" as an environment attribute "supplied by the requesting plane and attested where the platform can attest them," directly above load-bearing rule 1 "No self-asserted attributes" — time is the one decision input the corpus concedes is self-asserted with best-effort attestation. That is an internal tension inside one section, not an inference. (4) Layer 3 does not backstop it: §7.3's RLS consumes subject attributes as per-transaction SET LOCAL GUCs derived from the same Layer 2 subject context, and re-checks dominance, never freshness — so §7.3's "disclosure requires Layer 2 and Layer 3 to fail identically" is satisfied by one shared unattested input. (5) Worst placement is corpus-acknowledged: §7.2 permits the hook-B hot path to run as local maknae-dcs-core bindings inside `lake`, which container-architecture §2 rule 3 declares untrusted by design; an untrusted container's clock then bounds its own authorization window. Refutations attempted and failed: §5.1 "STIG-aligned session lifetimes" governs lifetime length not clock trust; RFC 8707 audience binding is anti-replay across resources, not time; KLC §11.3 revalidate_after is an object-tier freshness control on the dreaming cycle, not a subject-context control. No YAGNI/deny-by-default exclusion applies — deny-by-default is exactly what the gap inverts, and §9.1 already enumerates checks at this granularity (FIPS self-checks, RLS parity hash), so a clock-sanity check is at the right altitude.

findings.summary: maknae-tdf is a from-scratch cryptographic implementation consumed by the two architecture-defeating containers, but every assurance requirement D17 states is open-source ecosystem hygiene — no fuzzing of the attacker-facing unwrap path, no differential testing, no cryptographic review, no policy-binding-before-plaintext requirement.
findings.evidence: 'No unsafe without documented justification' gives memory safety, not cryptographic correctness: a safe-Rust implementation that releases plaintext before verifying the policy binding is the exact defect class, and nothing in D17 would catch it. §11 scopes TDF to objects that leave the platform boundary, so the unwrap path consumes attacker-controlled bundles by design. D17's 'zero Maknae coupling' removes the usual mitigation of scoping to the needed subset.
findings.recommendation: Add trust-plane assurance distinct from ecosystem hygiene: fuzzing of the manifest/unwrap parser as a release gate; differential testing against an existing OpenTDF SDK over the conformance vectors; an explicit tested requirement that policy-binding verification precedes any plaintext release; a cryptographic review before kernel/egress-proxy consumption (not merely before ecosystem submission); and a stated interim posture.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
Verified against the text, with one correction to the finding's wording that does not overturn it.

What the corpus actually says:
- §11 (line 273-274) does establish that `maknae-tdf` is trust-plane: "The containers that must wrap and unwrap — `kernel` and `egress-proxy` — are the two 100%-Rust trusted containers... moving label binding into a non-trust-plane language to dodge the gap is not acceptable." And §11's scope discipline confirms the attacker-facing direction: TDF is "the binding/wrapping layer for objects that leave the platform boundary (egress, replication, sneakernet bundles)" — so the unwrap path consumes externally-originated bundles by design.
- D17 (§16 line 363, expanded at §11 lines 277-281) lists exactly five assurance items: Rust API Guidelines, semver, rustdoc, MSRV policy, `cargo-audit`/`cargo-deny`, and "no `unsafe` without documented justification." Every one is ecosystem/supply-chain hygiene or memory safety. The finding's characterization is accurate, and ADR-0002's own honest boundary states the same limit in the corpus's voice: "logic errors, policy errors, and unsound `unsafe` in dependencies remain in scope — that is what the SA-11 test doctrine, the KLC §15 conformance vectors, and the dependency-vetting policy are for."
- The corpus's compensating assurance machinery does NOT reach this crate. §12's conformance vectors are explicitly label-semantics vectors ("KLC §15 invariants + lattice dominance cases + releasability/handling/NOFORN cases") over Maknae surfaces (`maknae-dcs-core`, Cedar policy set, generated RLS) — and D17's "zero Maknae coupling / never owns its API shape / no Maknae label vocabulary" affirmatively excludes the crate from that spine. container-architecture §5's TDD + mutation doctrine is scoped to "every container, every language"; `maknae-tdf` is deliberately not a container but an upstream-bound external dependency, so the "surviving mutants in trust-plane code are release blockers" gate does not clearly bind it. `grep -i fuzz` returns zero hits across the entire design corpus — so the specific gap the finding names (no fuzzing of an attacker-controlled parser) is verified by absence, not inferred.
- Correction: "no differential testing" slightly overstates. §11 does say the SDK is "validated against the OpenTDF spec's conformance materials." That is a spec-conformance obligation, and a refuter should credit it. But it is stated as a descriptive clause, not a release gate, it says nothing about differential behavior against an existing SDK on adversarial (as opposed to well-formed) inputs, and it cannot cover the ordering requirement — policy-binding verification before plaintext release — which is an internal control-flow property no conformance vector over valid bundles exercises. The finding's core claim survives this correction.

YAGNI/deny-by-default defense considered and rejected: the doc is v0.5 rough architecture and TDF is Phase B, which would excuse silence on undesigned matters — but D17 is not silence, it is an authored, dated decision record that enumerates the assurance posture and stops at hygiene. The corpus is asymmetric here: at the same maturity it commits to concrete, specific assurance elsewhere (RLS vectors executed against real PostgreSQL in CI, scheduled mutation runs as trust-plane release blockers, property tests naming partial-order axioms). A single named exception — the one from-scratch cryptographic implementation in the trust plane — receiving only ecosystem hygiene is a real gap in a decision record, not undesigned space.

Dependency on external fact: the recommendation's "policy-binding verification precedes plaintext release" presumes ZTDF's manifest carries a policy binding (an HMAC over the policy under the payload key) whose verification is separable from and can be misordered relative to payload decryption. I am confident this is true of the OpenTDF/TDF3 manifest structure, and the defect class (verify-then-release ordering) is generic to authenticated-encryption-plus-metadata formats regardless, so I do not downgrade to plausible on it. It should nonetheless be checked against github.com/opentdf/spec before the recommendation is written into an ADR.

Severity, re-assessed independently: should-fix, concurring. Not a blocker — nothing is built, Phase B entry is the natural insertion point, and the gap is an absent requirement rather than a stated-and-wrong one. Above discussion because it lands in a committed decision (D17) governing the trust plane's only from-scratch crypto, and because D17's own zero-coupling ruling is what severs the crate from the compensating conformance spine — the two rulings interact to create the hole, which is exactly the kind of thing an ADR amendment should record.

One refinement worth passing to the author: the cleanest framing is not "add five test requirements" but "state which assurance regime governs a trust-plane dependency that is deliberately outside Maknae's container/vector doctrine" — the structural question D17 left unanswered. Fuzzing, differential testing, binding-order, and pre-consumption crypto review are the contents; the missing thing is the regime.

findings.summary: The session high-water mark is asserted as the lattice join of retrieved inputs, but the untrusted runtime is what assembles the context; nothing requires the kernel to recompute the HWM from kernel-observed retrieval grants rather than from runtime-reported contents, enabling systematic under-marking.
findings.evidence: runtime is 'Untrusted by design' and holds persona-workspace rw; hook C's derivation is stated as a rule without naming the component that computes it or the evidence it uses.
findings.recommendation: Require the kernel to compute or independently audit the session HWM from its own record of hook-B grants at hook C, and treat a runtime-reported HWM as an untrusted hint that may only raise.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
I attempted to refute this against the corpus text and could not.

WHAT THE CORPUS ACTUALLY SAYS ABOUT HWM:
- abac §6.3 (line 154): "High-water-mark derivation — session/context rows are born labeled at the join (lattice max) of everything retrieved into them (hook C); internally born state is never unlabeled." Passive voice: no component named, no evidence source named.
- abac §3.1 (line 78) and container-arch §3.9 (line 70): session state "carries / born at the high-water mark of its inputs" — again passive, no locus.
- abac §7 walkthrough (line 206): "context assembles, labeled at the high-water mark of its inputs" — the assembling actor in that same sentence chain is the runtime/lake ("runtime requests retrieval (hook B) → lake ... filter per-subject → context assembles").
- abac §12 (line 293): a proptest that "high-water-mark derivation is a lattice join" — tests the math, not the provenance of the inputs the math consumes.
- KLC §10 hook C row (line 208): "Runtime creates new object from existing ones | New object tier = 3; tier_ceiling = min(ceiling of all inputs); full input lineage recorded" — the classification HWM is absent entirely (this is RL#1 blocker B13), and the actor named is the runtime.
- KLC §15: `derived_classification: high_water_mark_of_inputs` — an invariant with no bearer.

THE BEST REFUTATION CANDIDATES, AND WHY THEY FALL SHORT:
1. KLC §6 notes (line 101): "The kernel enforces dominance: no read up (hook B) and no write down (hooks C/E — a derived object classifies at the high-water mark of its inputs...)." This is the strongest counter-text and it does partially assign the locus (kernel enforces at hook C). But it says nothing about the *evidence base*: a kernel that computes the join over a runtime-supplied input list is still under-marked whenever the runtime omits an input. The finding's precise claim — nothing requires the kernel to derive the mark from its own record of hook-B grants — survives this sentence.
2. KLC §11.1 / §10 hook C "full input lineage recorded." Lineage is the natural evidence base, but the corpus never says who *authors* lineage, and it explicitly locks derived-only status only for `nature/domain/band/ceiling` (§6 notes; §15 `object_authority_fields: derived_only`) — classification/lineage are not covered by that lock. §15 lists `derived_classification` as a rule, not as a derived-only-input field. So lineage is exactly the forgeable input the finding describes (structurally identical to RL#1 B21's `issuance_type` "authored at ingest" defect).
3. container-arch principle 5 / abac §3.1 "the runtime touches state only through the kernel's decisions … working sets check in and out through kernel-mediated access." This is a real partial mitigation and is why I did not raise the severity to blocker. But abac §7.2 defines what "kernel-mediated" concretely means for the state store: PEPs holding a kernel-minted subject context that "injects label predicates into its queries," with the kernel deliberately kept "off the per-query hot path." Predicate injection constrains *which rows a subject may touch*; it does not validate that a written session row's classification equals the join of what was retrieved into it. Layer 3 (§7.3) is the same story — RLS enforces NOT NULL labels and dominance-for-the-subject, and its "failure mode is always fewer rows"; nothing in RLS can detect an under-marked row. So none of the three layers re-derives the mark.

CONSEQUENCE (why it matters, not just a wording gap): under-marking does not disclose to the operator anything hook B already denied them, so the read-up half is safe. The damage is on the write-down half, which is a headline claim of the corpus: hook E's endpoint dominance check (KLC line 102, abac §7 line 206, container-arch §3.2 "payload label screening") consumes the payload's *declared* mark. A runtime that reports a lower join routes SECRET//REL content to an endpoint accredited below it — the exact "data sovereignty holds when nobody is watching" property the corpus asserts — and equally launders `no-egress` handling caveats that §6.3 says propagate at hook C. The runtime is "Untrusted by design" (container-arch §2 row 4) and holds `persona-workspace` rw (§4), so this is not a hypothetical actor.

CLASS PLACEMENT: this is a genuine instance of RL#1's Class A ("enforcement asserted without a trust-plane locus"), sitting between B12 (no component specified as the trusted minter of classification labels), B13 (hook C row omits the HWM stamp), and B5 (handling caveats lack a propagation/taint model). It is not fully redundant with any of them: B13 is a two-representations/omission finding about the hook table's completeness; this is about the *integrity of the derivation's inputs* even once B13 is fixed by adding the missing row text. Fixing B13 as written (add "stamp classification HWM" to the hook C row) would NOT fix this — that is the test that establishes it as a distinct increment. The recommendation as written (kernel derives from its own hook-B grant record; runtime-reported mark is an untrusted hint that may only raise) is the correct shape and is consistent with RL#1's Class A redesign recommendation #1/#2 and the §11.4 doctrine "the runtime's good behavior is never the control; the kernel is."

SEVERITY: should-fix, held rather than raised. Independently it is blocker-grade in impact, but two things bound it: KLC line 101 does assign hook C enforcement to the kernel (so this is a specification-completeness gap on an already-stated kernel duty, not an outright missing gate), and the fix is a bounded design statement that lands naturally inside the already-docketed ADR-0004/0005 and ADR-0008 rather than requiring a new redesign class. It should be written into ADR-0005 (enforcement locus) with the lattice mechanics in ADR-0008; adr_candidate: true is correct.

EXTERNAL FLOOR: no. The kernel already observes every hook-B decision by construction (§7.1: all six hooks are Cedar evaluations in the kernel), so recomputing the join over its own grant record is a patchable seam, not an unreachable one. The genuine external floor nearby is a different residual — the RL#1 §6 one, that authorized content can still exfiltrate to a legitimately accredited endpoint — and this finding is not that.

No external fact is in doubt; everything here is verified against the corpus text itself, so this is 'confirmed' rather than 'plausible'.

findings.rl1_disposition: open — new instance of the still-live RL#1 Class A ("Enforcement asserted without a trust-plane locus" / privileged act sited in the untrusted plane). It is not among the 22 docketed blockers (B1–B22 cover corpus rw-mounts, hook loci, gateway trust, skill registry — not outbound credential acquisition), and it appears in newly authored text (`abac-dcs-architecture.md` v0.3, 2026-07-15) rather than in the reviewed RL#1 surface. Strictly: the class was never killed — the prescribed redesign ADRs (0004/0005) exist only as a proposed docket; `design/adr/` contains only ADR-0001/0002/0003. So this is Class A resurfacing at a fresh seam in a fresh document, which is evidence the class is a property of the design, not of any one passage.
findings.relocated_class: Class A — enforcement/privileged act placed in the untrusted (or under-specified) plane while surrounding text asserts the trust-plane property. Same class as RL#1 §2; resurfaced at a new seam (outbound credential acquisition) in a document authored after RL#1. Folds into the ADR-0005 enforcement-locus scope.
findings.summary: Outbound OAuth token acquisition is placed in gateway/runtime, and runtime is 'Untrusted by design' — so 'tokens are stored only in Vault' describes the resting state, not the handling path, and a compromised runtime obtains a durable model-provider credential usable outside the platform where hook E does not apply.
findings.evidence: Acquiring a token is performing a privileged act: the runtime would handle the authorization code, the token response and the refresh token, and be the writer of record into Vault — contradicting container §3.4's 'the runtime requests, never performs'. §15's IA-5(2) mapping is hard to sustain with the acquisition path in the untrusted plane. The residual is bounded (egress-proxy mediates in-platform use) but the credential itself leaks.
findings.recommendation: Move acquisition to the trust plane: the runtime requests an outbound connection; the kernel or egress-proxy performs the exchange, writes Vault, and injects the token at egress time. If acquisition must be interactive, say gateway (security-relevant), drop runtime from the sentence, state the gateway's credential-handling requirements, and record the residual.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
Verified against the text. `design/abac-dcs-architecture.md` §5.2 item 2 (line 130) reads: "**Outbound — Maknae as OAuth client**: model-provider subscription auth (MVP item 1) and MCP client connections (Security MCP first). Token acquisition lives in `gateway`/`runtime`; tokens are stored only in Vault, transit only the `egress-proxy`, and every outbound token use is a hook E decision."

Three independent confirmations:

1. **Trust-plane contradiction is textual, not inferred.** `container-architecture.md` §2 row 4 classes `runtime` as "Untrusted by design", and §1 principle 3 repeats it. §3.4 states "Every privileged act transits the kernel; the runtime requests, never performs, lifecycle transitions." Even reading the second clause narrowly (it is grammatically scoped to *lifecycle transitions*), the first clause — "Every privileged act transits the kernel" — is unqualified, and an OAuth authorization-code exchange that yields a durable refresh token is a privileged act. Naming `runtime` as an acquisition locus therefore contradicts the container doc's own principle.

2. **The sentence is internally inconsistent with itself.** "tokens ... transit only the `egress-proxy`" cannot hold if acquisition (the token *response*, including the refresh token) is handled in `gateway`/`runtime`. The token demonstrably transits at least one non-egress-proxy container on the acquisition path. This is a same-sentence defect, so no charitable reading rescues it; "stored only in Vault" describes the resting state, exactly as the finding says.

3. **Control-mapping strain is real.** §15 (line 329) maps the OAuth front door to IA-5(2) among others. Nothing in the corpus places outbound credential acquisition in the trust plane: §3.8 `vault-agent` covers secret *consumption* only ("services consume via native Vault API"), §3.2 `egress-proxy` is described as enforcement/PEP for outbound flows and is never named as the party that performs the token exchange or writes Vault, and §9.2's fail-closed matrix covers "Vault sealed" but not acquisition locus. §14 open item 4 concerns the *internal* service-to-service credential envelope, not this. So the corpus does not address it elsewhere — no refutation available on "already covered."

Refutation attempts that failed: (a) "gateway is the interaction plane, so an interactive code flow legitimately lands there" — plausible for `gateway` alone (Security-relevant, not Untrusted), but the sentence names `runtime` too, and the recommendation already concedes the gateway-only phrasing as an acceptable fix; (b) "YAGNI / MVP scope" — the doc itself tags model-provider subscription auth as **MVP item 1**, so it is in scope now; (c) "residual is negligible" — bounded in-platform (hook E + egress-proxy mediate *use*), but the exfiltrated refresh token is usable outside the platform where hook E does not apply, which is the finding's precise claim and it stands.

Severity held at **should-fix** rather than blocker: the leaked credential is a model-provider subscription secret, not a key to labeled data or the label-integrity root, and the platform-side data-confidentiality claims (Layers 2/3, hook E dominance, RLS) survive its loss. It is nonetheless a textual contradiction on the corpus's single load-bearing claim and belongs in the ADR-0005 (enforcement-locus / TCB boundary) scope, not in a prose patch alone.

Note on the fix: the recommendation's "egress-proxy performs the exchange" option should be weighed against §3.2's deliberate framing of the proxy as pure PEP ("the kernel decides, the proxy enforces") — making it a credential holder/Vault writer widens its job description. Kernel-performs-exchange (or a gateway-only interactive leg with a kernel-owned Vault write) fits the stated doctrine more cleanly.

findings.relocated_class: Lifecycle-tier arithmetic pressed into service as the decision machinery for a different axis. Same structural shape as RL#1 B18 (which ranks authority precedence by tier number, violating precedence_outside_typed_edges: never) — here tier demotion stands in for a confidentiality-label correction. B18 has not been redesigned, so the class has not been killed; this is the same class surfacing at a new seam (§10 spillage response), and it is entangled with B18's open "undefined below Tier 3" quarantine semantics, which is exactly what determines whether hooks B/F actually gate a quarantined row. Should be adjudicated with B18 under one "tier is not a security axis" ADR rather than as an independent item.
findings.summary: Spillage response is routed to the KLC's lifecycle-tier demotion machinery, which acts on the wrong axis: quarantining or purging a row does not correct a classification label that is too low, and no mechanism for raising a label exists anywhere in the corpus.
findings.evidence: §6.3 has just declared the axes orthogonal ('lifecycle answers how trusted; the lattice answers who may see'). Demoting a spilled row leaves its classification untouched, so it remains readable at all three layers. The correct remediation is an upgrade, which KLC §15's classification_downgrade_by_automation: never does not prohibit — yet 'No automated downgrade, ever' is cited as if it governed. No remediation path exists for prior exposure (contexts assembled from the row, audit rows that inherited the label, endpoints already routed under it), and 'purge' destroys the artifact needed to scope the spill.
findings.recommendation: Define a classification-elevation path in §10 with the kernel as sole writer, operator-signed and audited before/after, plus the downstream re-evaluation it triggers (recompute every row whose lineage includes the corrected object; enumerate egress events under the old label). Reserve tier demotion/purge for the trust axis; record as an ADR alongside the lattice ADR.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
CORE CONFIRMED, several sub-claims REFUTED; severity reduced.

Verified in text: (1) abac §10 L260 routes the entire spillage response to lifecycle-tier machinery ("quarantine, purge with retained audit record"); (2) §6.3 L149 + KLC §5 do declare the axes orthogonal ("lifecycle answers how trusted; the lattice answers who may see"); (3) tier demotion demonstrably leaves the classification label untouched; (4) grep across both docs for upgrade|elevat|reclassif|relabel confirms NO upward label-correction path exists — KLC §6 L101 defines only the downward direction ("Downgrade/sanitization is a signed act by an authorized subject — never automated"), and KLC §15 constrains only classification_downgrade_by_automation. So citing "No automated downgrade, ever (KLC §15)" at a remediation that would require an upward correction is a genuine non-sequitur: the cited invariant does not govern the act §10 needs.

Evidence the finding MISSED that strengthens it: §7.3's generated RLS predicate is "classification ordinal + releasability array containment + noforn + subject/handling_grants" — there is no tier term. The at-rest backstop is classification-axis-only, so a lifecycle-axis quarantine provably cannot reach Layer 3. A quarantined-but-underlabeled row stays visible to the independent backstop until purge. That is the concrete axis mismatch, and it is real.

Sub-claims REFUTED against the text: (a) "purge destroys the artifact needed to scope the spill" — §10 explicitly says "purge with retained audit record", quarantine is listed first as the non-destructive option, §10¶4 makes audit rows a labeled structured query surface, and KLC hook C records full input lineage, so the scoping machinery exists; (b) "no mechanism for producing a correctly-labeled object" — purge + re-ingest through hook A (which stamps labels and does the ceiling dominance check) is an existing composed path the finding never considers, and it is arguably safer than in-place mutation; (c) "the correct remediation is an upgrade" is over-broad — in the canonical DoD spillage case (content whose true label exceeds the instance ceiling) an in-place upgrade is PROHIBITED by hook A/the ceiling and purge is doctrinally correct, so routing to purge is not simply wrong-axis; (d) "remains readable at all three layers" is asserted, not demonstrated — hook B carries a "task's minimum tier satisfied" condition, so Layers 1/2 plausibly do deny a quarantined row (its force depends on RL#1 B18's already-open "undefined below Tier 3" defect); only Layer 3 is provably unreached.

RESIDUAL DEFECT (what I confirm): §10 does not distinguish the two spillage subcases (mislabeled-but-holdable vs. above-ceiling), defines no in-place label-correction path for the former, specifies no downstream re-evaluation, and mis-cites a downgrade invariant as governing. The sharpest un-remediable piece is one the finding gestures at but under-argues: hook C derived rows carry high-water marks computed from a too-low input and nothing recomputes them, and §10¶4 audit rows inherited the too-low label into an APPEND-ONLY store — those cannot be relabeled by any mechanism the corpus describes, even after the source row is purged. Persistent residual misclassification in a system whose sole purpose is classification enforcement.

Severity: should-fix, not blocker. Downgraded because the finding's central premise (nothing can yield a correctly-labeled object) is wrong, and because the fallback the doc does specify (purge) is fail-closed and destroys the exposure rather than perpetuating it. It remains a strong should-fix and legitimately ADR-worthy, since the append-only audit contamination has no path at all.

findings.rl1_disposition: open — B11 is untouched, not killed and not relocated. Nothing in the 2026-07-15 abac document redesigns the output path; the per-operator session/state-store work (abac §3.1, §7.2) resolves the 1:1 half by scoping context to a subject, but the shared-channel half and the fork/merge half of B11 have no text anywhere in the corpus. ADR-0009 ("Output-interface MLS model — no-write-down on replies to operators; shared-channel floor labels; context fork/merge") remains docketed and unwritten.
findings.summary: RL#1 B11 is untouched and sharpened: the enforcement points are enumerated as egress-proxy, data-access layers and skill sandbox, and web-ui 'displays, never enforces' — so the path by which a composed reply reaches a human has no PEP by construction, and shared channels have no floor label.
findings.evidence: §8.1 ends 'response rendered; audit events at every hop' with no recipient-dominance check; §8.2 addresses only retrieval. Partial progress: per-operator session state resolves the 1:1 half of B11, but a channel where several operators with different attributes read the same rendered reply remains unspecified, and no floor-label concept exists in the new document.
findings.recommendation: Make operator-facing output a first-class enforcement point: a distinct output hook, or an explicit hook E rule that every authenticated recipient's attributes must dominate the reply payload's high-water mark, with shared channels bound to a floor label (greatest lower bound of members) capping what a serving context may contain. Add the multi-operator reply case to §12's negative tests.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
I tried to refute this on three fronts and it survives, but the finding overstates one clause and I narrow it accordingly.

REFUTATION ATTEMPT 1 — "the corpus already puts a PEP on the render path." Partially successful. `container-architecture.md` §3.2 (`egress-proxy`) states: "model-endpoint calls (OAuth subscription + OpenAI-compatible registrations), learning fetches, and **channel egress** all transit it; the kernel decides, the proxy enforces (PEP). Holds the Hook E data path." Since `gateway` (§3.3) is a Discord/Matrix **channel adapter**, the reply-to-human path for the MVP delivery mode *does* cross a declared PEP. KLC §5 likewise asserts "retrieval (hook B), skill execution (hook F), and **outputs (hook E)** are all filtered per subject," and §6 gives "no write down (hooks C/E — ... a task context assumes the high-water mark of everything retrieved into it; **its outputs inherit that mark**)." So the finding's strongest phrasing — "no PEP by construction" — is **not accurate for channel delivery**, and `web-ui` is post-MVP (container-arch §2, deferred) with the read path still crossing hook B + RLS. That clause should be struck.

REFUTATION ATTEMPT 2 — "hook E's rule set already covers it." Fails. KLC §10 hook E enumerates: destination on authority map or task-scoped allowlist; no `no-egress` content; Tier ≤ 1 quoting requires explicit rule; **model-endpoint** eligibility = subject attributes × endpoint labels × payload labels. Every dominance rule in the corpus is written against *model endpoints* as labeled resources (KLC §6 bullet 3; abac §8.1 "hook E ... requires an endpoint whose labels dominate the payload mark"). There is no rule that a **human recipient's** attributes must dominate the payload, and no notion of a channel/destination carrying a label at all — a Discord channel satisfies hook E as a bare allowlisted destination. So the enforcement machinery is anchored (locus exists) but the *rule content* for human recipients is genuinely absent. abac §8.1's flow terminates at "response rendered; audit events at every hop" with no dominance check on the render step, and §3 pins `web-ui` as "displays, never enforces" — confirmed against the text.

REFUTATION ATTEMPT 3 — "YAGNI / deny-by-default legitimately excludes it." Fails. Deny-by-default answers the *cross-persona* question (KLC §14 Q7, rescoped to single-persona MVP), but the same note explicitly says the operative near-term requirement is "**multi-operator DCS filtering of the single agent**," and abac §8.1 closes with a multi-operator scenario on the same instance. A Discord/Matrix channel is multi-reader by nature, so the shared-destination case is in MVP scope, not deferred. Deny-by-default also does not supply a floor: with no channel label, there is nothing to deny *against*. Nothing in abac §16 (D1–D17) or §17 (Q1–Q7) touches output MLS or channel labels; §12's negative tests list (REL drift, cross-subject health query, NOFORN at a foreign endpoint, tampered SPIF) has no multi-recipient reply case.

NET: the defect is real but should be restated as **"hook E has no recipient-dominance rule and destinations-to-humans are unlabeled"** rather than "no enforcement locus exists." The fix is cheap and already-shaped: channel destinations become labeled resources exactly like model endpoints, with a floor label = greatest lower bound of authenticated members, and hook E's dominance check generalizes from endpoint-labels to destination-labels. That reuse is why this is should-fix rather than blocker — and it is exactly ADR-0009's docketed scope, which is unwritten.

findings.relocated_class: Same Class A shape, one seam further along: the lifecycle/integrity axis is no longer merely unstated — it is now present as first-class schema (§6.3) and as per-object hook conditions (KLC §10 B/E/F) while the newly ratified three-layer enforcement architecture, the SPIF-generated RLS predicate set, and the property-test spine are built exclusively on the confidentiality axis. The class relocated from "constraint asserted with no enforcement locus" to "constraint given a data representation but still no aggregate enforcement locus" — not killed.
findings.summary: RL#1 B9 is untouched and the asymmetry is now structural: all three enforcement layers, the RLS predicate set and the entire conformance spine are confidentiality-only, with no predicate anywhere consuming the lifecycle/integrity axis the same document names.
findings.evidence: §7.3's predicate carries no tier or provenance term; §12's vectors and property tests assert nothing about Tier-3 content steering a privileged action; §9.2 has no row for a privileged action requested from a quarantine-tainted context; and §4's environment-attribute list — the one place a context-integrity input could have been declared — omits it. The confused-deputy residual is unchanged.
findings.recommendation: Declare the integrity dual even if MVP defers enforcement: a context-integrity attribute (minimum tier of everything that influenced the context) as a fourth Cedar context input, hook F's rule over it (a tainted context gets a reduced whitelist or requires operator approval for state-changing skills), and at least one negative vector so the gap is visible in CI. If accepted as a residual, register it in §9.2 rather than leaving KLC §8 step 3's promise standing.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
Verified against the text; the defect is real but the finding's summary overstates it and should be narrowed.

CONFIRMED elements (checked line-by-line):
- §7.3's RLS predicate set is enumerated exhaustively ("dominance predicate over the classification ordinal + releasability array containment + `noforn` + `subject`/`handling_grants` join") and carries no tier, ceiling, or provenance term.
- §4's environment-attribute list — time, network location, host/sandbox posture, channel origin — omits any context-integrity input, and §4 is explicitly the place the third input class is "named explicitly."
- §9.2's fail-closed matrix (8 rows) has no row for a privileged action requested from a quarantine-influenced context.
- §12's property tests (dominance partial order, HWM lattice join, RLS predicate monotonicity) are confidentiality-axis only, and §12's negative testing is generated from §9.2 rows, inheriting that gap.
- §6.3 assigns context/session rows a confidentiality high-water mark ("born labeled at the join (lattice max) of everything retrieved into them") with no integrity dual. KLC §11.1's `tier_ceiling = min(inputs)` applies to derived *objects*, never to contexts — so no aggregate integrity term exists for the thing that steers an action.
- design/adr/ contains only ADR-0001..0003; ADR-0010 does not exist. reviews/RL-convergence-ledger.md:63 carries "Quarantine integrity-taint | 5 findings | ⏳ | ADR-0010, #8" — tracked as pending, not addressed. §17's open questions do not list it either.

PARTIALLY REFUTED (the summary's absolutist framing, not the defect):
- "all three enforcement layers ... no predicate anywhere consuming the lifecycle/integrity axis" is false as written. §7.1 states "All six KLC hooks are Cedar evaluations," and KLC §10 hooks B, E, F carry explicit tier predicates ("Task's minimum tier satisfied"; "Tier ≤ 1 content quoted outbound requires explicit rule"; "Skill signed and at executable tier"). Layer 1 therefore does consume the lifecycle axis at object granularity.
- "the entire conformance spine is confidentiality-only" is false. §12 seeds vectors from "KLC §15 invariants," of which roughly half are lifecycle-axis (all_new_knowledge_enters_at_tier: 3, promotion_step_size_max: 1, tier_ceiling_raised_by_automation: never, derived_ceiling: min_of_inputs, unsigned_skill_execution: deny).

The surviving, precise defect: what is absent is an AGGREGATE context-integrity term — the minimum tier of everything that influenced a context — not the tier axis wholesale. Per-object tier gating exists; the taint aggregate that hook F would need to refuse a privileged action from a Tier-3-influenced context does not exist at any layer, in any vector, or in any environment attribute. That is exactly B9's confused-deputy residual, and the new architecture document — which ratifies the enforcement layers, the RLS predicate set, and the conformance spine — hardens the asymmetry by building all three on the confidentiality axis while §6.3 names the lifecycle axis as first-class schema. The recommendation (declare the dual as a fourth Cedar context input + a hook-F rule + at least one negative vector, or register it in §9.2 as an accepted residual) is proportionate and correct.

Severity: should-fix is right, not blocker. The document is an explicitly rough v0.5 architecture with a live open-questions section and a convergence ledger that already homes this family to ADR-0010/#8, so it is tracked rather than silently dropped; but the ledger entry does not appear in the architecture document itself, and §9.2 is the document's own residual/failure register — so the promise in KLC §8 step 3 ("may inform the current task's reasoning but not privileged actions") still stands with no enforcement locus anywhere in the ratified enforcement architecture.

findings.section: §13 Phase A ('signed-git label integrity'), §11 (OpenTDF binding), §9.1 vs KLC §6, §12
findings.rl1_disposition: open — B7 is untouched: no ADR-0007, no signed-payload definition, no import freshness/revision/revocation binding. Strictly this is not a relocation (nothing was redesigned away); it is the original blocker still open, with the class widened — the new ABAC document adds a third label-integrity name ("signed-git label integrity", §11) and a fourth (OpenTDF binding, §11 Phase B) without defining the payload, key trust, or composition of any of them. Borderline blocker: it stays should-fix only because the corpus is an explicitly rough draft and §11/§13 are honest that cryptographic binding is Phase B; the load-bearing part — §11 asserting an undefined signed-git control as a shipped Phase-A property while §9.1 boot validation has no object-integrity check — should be raised before any implementation commit.
findings.relocated_class: Signature-as-control with undefined payload, key trust and lifecycle semantics — retained in full and widened by additional undefined mechanism names, not relocated to a new seam
findings.summary: RL#1 B7 is unresolved and a third label-integrity mechanism now exists — signed-git label integrity (Phase A), KLC detached signatures for tier <= 1, and OpenTDF binding (Phase B) — with no statement of which is authoritative, how they compose, or what payload any of them signs.
findings.evidence: The signed byte range over mutable frontmatter is still undefined, so promotion/demotion either orphans signatures or cannot attest tiers, and KLC §12's import path still has no freshness, revision counter or revocation binding — a stale signature attesting a former tier remains valid on import. §9.1's boot checks cover only the authority map and attribute store; no check covers object or state-store row integrity, and state-store labels rest on NOT NULL plus RLS with no integrity mechanism. §2.1 meanwhile answers the STANAG binding requirement with a Phase-B mechanism the MVP does not have.
findings.recommendation: Author the key/signature ADR before Phase B and make it the single source: canonical signed structure (content hash, id, type, tier, tier_ceiling, classification, key id, monotonic revision), re-sign on promotion, kernel-countersigned supersession on demotion, import honouring only the latest revision under the receiving trust anchors. State in §11/§13 that signed-git and TDF binding are transports for that structure, not alternatives, say what protects state-store row labels, and mark Phase A's threat model as excluding cryptographic binding.
findings.verifier_reasoning: Verified directly against the text. (1) design/adr/ holds only ADR-0001..0003 — the RL#1-recommended ADR-0007 (key & signature model, resolving B7 + #25) was never authored, so B7 is untouched. (2) KLC §6 still declares `signatures: []  # required for tier <= 1; detached sigs, operator or CI key` with no canonicalization or signed byte range, over a frontmatter block containing the mutable `tier`, `freshness.last_validated` and provenance fields — the exact B7 dilemma (sig orphaned on every transition, or unable to attest tier) is intact. (3) KLC §12 says receiving sites "re-verify signatures before honoring tiers" with no revision counter, freshness or revocation binding, so a stale signature attesting a former (higher) tier survives import — tier resurrection stands. (4) The third mechanism is real: abac §11 asserts "MVP ships the schema, RLS, and signed-git label integrity" as a shipped Phase-A control that is defined nowhere; the only other use of signed-git (§3, line 82) scopes it strictly to Tier-0 configuration (authority map, operator attributes, SPIF, endpoint registrations), never to object labels. No text in any of the three documents states which of signed-git integrity, KLC detached signatures, or OpenTDF/STANAG-4778 binding is authoritative, or how they compose. (5) abac §9.1's seven boot-blocking checks cover SPIF well-formedness, authority-map and attribute-store signatures, Cedar schema/vectors, RLS parity hash, FIPS self-test and instance ceiling — none covers lake-object or state-store row integrity. (6) abac §7.3 protects state-store labels with NOT NULL + FORCE RLS + deny-all + no BYPASSRLS: access control and non-nullability, not integrity, on a store container-architecture itself calls "data plane, untrusted-adjacent". Partial refutation, non-fatal: the finding's §2.1 clause overreaches — §2.1 explicitly says "Schema-ready at MVP (ported label_id placeholder); binding lands with OpenTDF (§11); ACP 240 conformance claimed only after the document is in hand", and §11's scope-discipline paragraph defers binding to Phase B, so the phasing is disclosed honestly rather than answered with a mechanism the MVP pretends to have; that clause should be dropped from the write-up. Minor citation slip: the "signed-git label integrity" phrase is in §11, not in the §13 Phase A row, whose text never mentions it. Neither defect in the write-up rescues the corpus. No YAGNI/deny-by-default defence is available: doctrine 2 ("Absence of a rule, an attribute, a label, a signature, or a reachable decision point is a denial") makes signature semantics load-bearing, and RL#1 already ranked the key model as the highest-value should-fix and ADR-0007 as foundational.

findings.summary: RL#1 B14/B19 are untouched and the new conformance spine cannot reach them: it is scoped to §15 invariants plus lattice cases, and §15 contains no corroboration or session-independence invariant — while the redesign built the very evidence store that would make those checks mechanical and wired nothing to it.
findings.evidence: The 2→1 document gate and the memory ≥3-independent-sessions gate stay outside the only declared acceptance test, with §14 Q8 still undecided. §3.1 now puts sessions and the memory index in a queryable store and §6.3 carries provenance/lineage on those rows — exactly what a lineage-disjointness check needs.
findings.recommendation: State the mechanical independence floor now, independent of Q8: corroborating objects must have distinct registry issuers, disjoint lineage closures and no common non-Tier-≤1 ancestor; counted sessions must trace to disjoint source closures. Add them as KLC §15 invariants so they enter the §12 spine, and change the §9.1 parenthetical to '(independence: OPEN — §14 Q8)'.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
Verified directly against the text; every load-bearing claim holds.

1. Spine scope: abac §12 defines the vectors as "KLC §15 invariants + lattice dominance cases + releasability/handling/NOFORN cases"; container-architecture §6 (line 110) states the same scope verbatim ("KLC §15 invariants plus lattice dominance cases"). Negative testing in §12 is enumerated as the §9.2 fail-closed matrix rows and the §8 worked flows. Nothing in either list reaches KLC §9.1 promotion gates. D15 nevertheless declares these "the single conformance spine."

2. §15 content: the invariant block (KLC lines 268–289) contains 14 entries. Promotion-adjacent ones exist (`promotion_step_size_max: 1`, `tier_0_writes: operator_signature_only`, `all_new_knowledge_enters_at_tier: 3`), but there is NO corroboration invariant and NO session-independence invariant. So the 2→1 document gate and the ≥3-independent-sessions memory gate are provably outside the only declared acceptance test — the finding's central mechanism is textually established, not inferred.

3. B14/B19 untouched: KLC §9.1 still reads "second independent ceiling-1 source (independence definition: §14 Q8)" and "Confirmed across ≥3 independent sessions"; §14 Q8 still reads "*Operator: undecided as of 2026-07-14.*" The KLC revision history ends at 0.2 (2026-07-14) — the document was not modified in the round that produced the abac v0.5 redesign. A grep for "independen|corrobor" across the whole corpus finds no other definition; abac's §16 decision log and §17 open questions do not touch it.

4.
