findings.verifier_reasoning:
Verified against the text; I tried three refutation routes and none held.

**The dual encoding is real and in the text.** container-architecture.md §5 line 99: "**KLC §15 invariants become executable property tests** in every container that touches labels — the machine-readable block is the shared acceptance suite, **implemented once per language** and run in CI," backed by a 4-language toolchain matrix (proptest / hypothesis / rapid / fast-check, lines 92–95). container-architecture.md §6 line 110: "**Conformance vectors are the enforcement.** KLC §15 invariants plus lattice dominance cases ship as **language-neutral golden test vectors** in this repo; every implementation … must pass the identical vectors in CI." abac-dcs-architecture.md §12 line 285: "**Conformance vectors are the single spine.** Language-neutral golden vectors (**KLC §15 invariants** + lattice dominance cases + …)." So the same source block (KLC §15's `klc_invariants` YAML, lines 273–288) is declared to be encoded both as one language-neutral vector corpus AND as N hand-implemented per-language suites. "Implemented once per language" is explicitly *implementation*, not generation — §6's codegen rule is scoped to representation only ("The `dcs_label` block and the kernel decision request/response protocol are versioned schemas … per-language types are generated, never hand-rolled") and does not cover invariants.

**Refutation attempt 1 — "they're complementary test kinds, not duplicate representations."** Partly true and worth carrying: abac §12's property tests are algebraic laws (partial order, lattice join, RLS monotonicity) that a fixed golden vector cannot express, and that paragraph is `proptest`-only (Rust). But container-architecture §5 does *not* frame its per-language suites as algebraic complements — it says the §15 block IS "the shared acceptance suite, implemented once per language," which is the same acceptance role §6/§12 assign to the vectors. Two artifacts claiming to be the acceptance encoding of one invariant list is the class, regardless of test technique.

**Refutation attempt 2 — "the corpus already has the update rule."** §5 line 99 does end with "A contract change without a corresponding test change fails review by definition." This is a genuine mitigation but does not refute: it is a human-review rule, singular ("a corresponding test change"), and binds neither the golden vectors nor the per-language suites specifically, nor is there any CI gate checking either artifact against the §15 YAML. No parity hash, checksum, or generation step covers the §15→vectors seam (contrast §6.4/§7.3's explicit SPIF→RLS parity check at kernel boot — the corpus knows how to build such a gate and did not build one here).

**Refutation attempt 3 — "§6's one-crate strategy makes the per-language suites vacuous."** §6 layer 3 ("Local evaluation is one Rust crate with bindings — never a port"; "Five of six containers never evaluate policy") does shrink where per-language invariant tests could even differ. But this *sharpens* rather than kills the finding: §5's mandate for per-language §15 invariant suites is in tension with §6's claim that only one implementation evaluates, which is an additional unreconciled seam in the same paragraph pair.

**Narrowing of the recommendation (the finding overstates one thing).** "Derive both suites from one machine-readable source" reads as if no such source exists — KLC §15 already *is* a machine-readable YAML block explicitly offered as acceptance criteria ("MUST hold in any implementation and MAY be used as acceptance criteria"). The correct fix is narrower: declare the §15 block normatively canonical, generate the golden vectors from it (or gate their agreement in CI), and state that per-language suites consume the vectors rather than re-encoding the invariant list — plus reconcile §5's "implemented once per language" against §6's one-crate-with-bindings rule.

**Severity — should-fix, held.** Blast radius is bounded: the vectors carry declared primacy ("the enforcement," "the single spine") and are run identically across implementations, so a drifted per-language suite degrades to redundant coverage rather than a missed denial — provided the vectors themselves track §15. That proviso is the ungated seam, and this corpus's own doctrine treats "N places that must stay in sync" as a class to kill, not patch. Cheap to fix at design stage (one normative sentence + a CI gate), expensive once four language suites exist. Not a blocker: no stated invariant is currently contradicted, only unreconciled.

findings.verifier_reasoning:
Verified against the text; I tried to refute it three ways and could not.

1) The invariant is still present and unamended. `knowledge-lifecycle-contract.md` §15 (line 274) reads `all_new_knowledge_enters_at_tier: 3` with no exemption clause. The only adjacent invariant, `tier_0_writes: operator_signature_only`, is an *authorization* rule (who may write Tier 0), not an *entry-tier* exemption — it does not rescue the contradiction. The revision history stops at 0.2 (2026-07-14), and the RL-convergence-ledger has no entry for redesign 0006, so the RL#1 remedy is recommended, not applied.

2) Both original contradicting surfaces are still live and are mutually exclusive with the invariant, not merely in tension:
- §7 (line 106): "The authority map ... is a Tier 0 artifact ... authored by the operator during onboarding." Combined with §5 (line 61): "There is no path from Tier 3 directly to Tier 0." So an operator-authored Tier-0 artifact provably cannot have entered at tier 3 and climbed — the invariant and the bootstrap path cannot both hold.
- §12: "receiving sites re-verify signatures before honoring tiers. A tier claim without a valid signature degrades to quarantine on import" — the explicit contrapositive is that a *validly signed* tier claim is honored above 3 on import. Note §12 also says sneakernet bundles "enter at Tier 3", so §12 itself carries both readings; the section is internally split, which strengthens rather than weakens the finding.

3) The third surface is real, not invented by the reviewer. `abac-dcs-architecture.md` §6.2 states the one logical schema has two physical projections — YAML frontmatter on lake objects and "**DCS columns** on state-store rows (sessions, tasks, memory index, audit)" — and §6.3 adds to that schema the "**KLC lifecycle axis** — `tier`, `tier_ceiling`, provenance/lineage, freshness". So state-store rows are specified to carry `tier`/`tier_ceiling` columns. Nothing in §3.1, §6.3, §7.3 or KLC §6/§7.2 states what tier those rows are born at, or how `tier_ceiling` derives for a row that has no issuer and therefore no (band, nature) pair to project over (§7.2 / KLC line 121). §3.1's "born at the high-water mark of its inputs" governs the *classification* axis only — KLC §5's own ruling is that the two axes are orthogonal, so it cannot be read as answering the tier question.

Attempted refutations that failed:
- "Hook C covers it": KLC §10 hook C sets "New object tier = 3" for runtime-derived objects, which could plausibly cover session rows. But it does not cover operator-created scheduler task definitions (created, not derived) or kernel-emitted audit rows, and neither §6.3 nor §3.1 invokes hook C for state-store row creation. Partial at best.
- "State-store rows aren't KLC knowledge objects": defensible as a *fix*, but the corpus does not say it — it says the opposite (§6.2/§6.3 give them the lifecycle axis), and §3.1's boundary paragraph only rules out the store being a shadow *Lake*, not that its rows are outside KLC.
- YAGNI/deny-by-default: does not excuse this. The contradiction's failure mode is fail-*closed* (a literal implementation of §15 refuses the authority-map bootstrap), so deny-by-default doctrine does not resolve it — it makes the system unbootstrappable rather than unsafe.

Severity re-assessed down from blocker to should-fix. The stakes are real — RL#1 remedy 0006 designates §15 + the §10 hook table as the canonical enforcement spec and explicitly says these are usable "as acceptance criteria" (§15 preamble), so an implementer generating tests from §15 gets a suite that rejects the system's own Tier-0 bootstrap. But there is no adversarial exploit and no fail-open: every reading of the contradiction denies rather than admits. It is a localized spec defect with a known, mechanical remedy (one exemption clause plus one normative sentence on platform-generated state), which is should-fix territory, not blocker. It becomes a blocker only if §15 is shipped as literal machine-consumed acceptance criteria before amendment.

The recommendation as written is correct and sufficient. One addition worth making: whichever branch is chosen for state-store rows, §7.2's ceiling projection needs an explicit issuer-less case, otherwise `tier_ceiling` is underived for every platform-generated row even after the entry tier is fixed.

findings.verifier_reasoning:
Verified the load-bearing evidence directly; one characterization in the finding is wrong but not load-bearing.

CONFIRMED against the text:
- `README.md` line 11 reads exactly `| **License** | TBD (MIT leaning, pending team decision) |`, and `ls` of the repo root shows no LICENSE file (root contains only README.md, design/, .git). `gh repo view` confirms `licenseInfo: null`.

The oauth-compliance.md and nato-dcra-acp240-findings.md headers state provenance and "read-only snapshot" but carry no permission/authorization statement and no license grant. Each retains its own author/security-contact block (oauth-compliance.md: "Author: Alex Ackerman", "Security Contact: security@securitymcp.io").

The corpus consistently calls the origin "the operator's Security MCP Server repository," the named author (Alex Ackerman) is Maknae's architect/owner per README line 10, and one import states the shared-author authorization explicitly. This is same-author/in-family content, not third-party redistribution — which is exactly the RL#1 relocated_class ("license diligence applied only to external upstreams, never to operator-owned repos"), so the class fit survives, but the alarm level in the summary is overstated.

findings.section: §11 scoping ruling / D17, §13 Phase B, §17 Q7 vs container-architecture.md §2, §6
findings.summary: D17 makes the SDK strictly larger than Maknae needs ('zero Maknae coupling'), adds open-source maintainership obligations to a three-architect team, and is the only major workstream in the corpus with no derisking or descope path — inconsistent with the YAGNI discipline applied everywhere else.
findings.evidence: container §2 ('never speculatively'), §6's two-step crate derisking and §13's 'apparatus activated when the consuming code exists' are the corpus's stated discipline. D17 forecloses the ordinary mitigation (implement the ZTDF subset the egress path uses) and adds semver, MSRV, rustdoc, a pluggable crypto backend for other people's requirements, naming coordination and an ongoing external relationship, while §17 Q7 shows the technical scope is still undetermined.
findings.recommendation: Add the derisking §6 gives the other crate: a pre-Phase-B re-verification trigger with automatic descope if an upstream Rust SDK exists; a two-step shape (narrow internal wrap/unwrap path first, ecosystem-grade generalization as a separately scheduled second step); a stated branch if OpenTDF-org coordination declines; and the maintainership obligation recorded as an ongoing roadmap cost.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
Verified against the text, but narrowed — one clause of the detail is refuted.

WHAT HOLDS:
1. D17's scope excess is real and literal. abac-dcs-architecture.md §11 (the "Scoping ruling" block) and the D17 row in §16 commit, "in force from the first commit," to: Rust API Guidelines checklist, semver discipline, full rustdoc, declared MSRV policy, cargo-audit/cargo-deny, zero Maknae coupling, a *pluggable, feature-gated crypto backend* explicitly so "the upstream ecosystem should not be forced onto Maknae's FIPS choice," a neutral submitted name coordinated with the OpenTDF organization, and an early external-organization approach. Several of these (pluggable non-FIPS backend, naming coordination, ecosystem API stewardship, ongoing maintainership) serve other people's requirements, not Maknae's egress/replication wrap-unwrap need. README line 10: team is "Alex (architect/owner) + two engineers."
2. The YAGNI inconsistency is textual, not inferred. README principle 5: "Propose the minimum that satisfies the contract; flag speculative scope as such." D17 is knowingly more than the minimum and is nowhere flagged as speculative or costed. container-architecture.md §6 gives the sibling crate (maknae-dcs-core) an explicit two-step derisked provenance ((a) in-repo lib crate, binary behavior unchanged, existing suite proves it; (b) lift to a shared home once the public API stabilizes) plus a bounded pre-step survey. abac §13 states "apparatus activated when the consuming code exists." maknae-tdf receives none of this apparatus: no re-verification trigger for the "verified 2026-07-15" crates.io gap before Phase B actually begins (§14's required-references table gates final design on the OpenTDF *spec*, not on whether an upstream Rust SDK appeared in the interim), no stated branch if OpenTDF-org coordination declines or imposes contribution requirements the team can't meet, no two-step narrow-then-generalize shape, and no maintainership obligation recorded as a roadmap cost. reviews/RL1-findings-digest.json has zero hits for tdf/OpenTDF/maintainer, so nothing upstream covers it either.
3. An aggravator the finding understates: a feature-gated *pluggable* crypto backend inside a crate consumed by kernel and egress-proxy is a build-configuration seam in the trust plane, where container-architecture §3.1/§3.2 make FIPS aws-lc-rs non-negotiable. That is a security-adjacent cost of the ecosystem-grade posture, not merely a schedule cost.

WHAT IS REFUTED (strike from the finding):
- "D17 forecloses the ordinary mitigation (implement the ZTDF subset the egress path uses)." It does not. "Zero Maknae coupling" governs API shape and vocabulary ("No Maknae label vocabulary, no kernel types"), not spec coverage; a spec-conformant ZTDF-manifest subset with zero Maknae coupling is fully consistent with D17.
- "§17 Q7 shows the technical scope is still undetermined" is used as an aggravator when Q7 ("ZTDF manifest subset first or nanoTDF first") is in fact a partial narrow-first descope lever already on the record. The recommendation's first step is therefore already half-present; what is missing is the *second* step (ecosystem-grade generalization scheduled separately) and the exit ramps.

Net: the defect survives as a roadmap/scope-governance gap — the one major workstream deliberately sized beyond the contract carries no re-verification trigger, no descope branch, and no recorded ongoing cost, in a corpus that derisks its sibling crate explicitly. The recommendation should be trimmed to the three genuinely missing items (pre-Phase-B upstream re-verification with automatic descope; declared branch if org coordination declines; maintainership + pluggable-backend cost recorded on the roadmap), since the "narrow subset first" ask is largely already Q7.

Severity held at discussion, not raised: the posture is an explicit operator ruling on a post-MVP phase, nothing at MVP is defeated, and the ask is derisking/documentation rather than a design change. No external fact is load-bearing — whether an upstream Rust OpenTDF SDK exists today is precisely what the recommended re-verification trigger would answer, so the recommendation stands either way.

findings.evidence: NIST.SP.800-207 §3.3 carries the quoted subject-database/role sentence verbatim; the DoD ICAM RD's 'Core Authorization Attributes' section is entirely 'Reserved for future version' and contains no mention of UIAS; CNSSI 4009 (2021) reference 91 is the ICTS UIAS v2.1; the ICAM RD lists 800-162, 800-205 and NISTIR 8112 by title and URL; AC-3(3)'s discussion names Bell-LaPadula. findings.verifier_reasoning:
I attempted to refute each of the five verification-record claims and could not; all check out against the lake-held originals, and the one caveat is confirmed against the corpus text.

Verified independently (lake at `/Users/thaChuck/_devops/projects/mpe-es/github-mpe-es/knowledgebase/`):
1. SP 800-207 quotation — `NIST.SP.800-207.md:1955` carries "…privileges should be assigned to a subject on an individual basis and not simply because they may fit into a particular role in the organization" verbatim, inside the §3.2 "Subject database" bullet. The §2.1 row's paraphrase ("trust-algorithm inputs include a subject database of attributes") is also accurate to that bullet. Minor: the finding cites §3.3; the bullet sits in the core-components list (Figure 2 descriptions, p.18) — a section-number slip in the *finding*, not in the corpus.
2. ICAM RD "Core Authorization Attributes" — `DoD_Enterprise_ICAM_Reference_Design.md:5457` is literally the heading followed by "Reserved for future version" and nothing else. No UIAS mention anywhere in that file. §2.1's provenance note is exactly right.
3. CNSSI 4009 UIAS provenance — `CNSSI_4009_FinalVersion_Clean_6December2021.md:13643` reference 91 = "Intelligence Community Technical Specification (ICTS), Unified Identity Attribute Set (UIAS) v2.1"; IC-sourced definitions (attribute service, authoritative attribute source, persona) are tagged "UIAS v2.1"/"ICTS UIAS v2.1". Confirms UIAS is IC vocabulary, supporting §4's "profile, not base standard" posture.
4. ICAM RD citing 800-162 / 800-205 / NISTIR 8112 — present by title and csrc URL at lines 903–908 and again at 1633–1635. §2.1's "cited through the ICAM RD's normative references" is accurate.
5. The PA caveat — CONFIRMED against the text. `abac-dcs-architecture.md:34` states the requirement as "PE/PA/PEP separation" and answers "Kernel = PE; PEPs throughout" — PA is named in the requires column and dropped in the answer; the §3 ABAC decomposition table likewise has PIP/PDP/PEP rows and no PA row.

Attempted refutation of the caveat, and the result: SP 800-207 (p.9) explicitly permits fusion — "Some implementations may treat the PE and PA as a single service; here, it is divided into its two logical components." So Maknae is *conformant*; the finding's own framing ("incomplete rather than wrong") survives this and is the correct characterization. The caveat is not refutable as a factual matter — the mapping row genuinely omits a role it itself names.

Where the finding under-sells itself: 800-207's PA definition is precisely "generate any session-specific authentication token or credential used by a client" and "if… a previous approval is countermanded, the PA signals to the PEP to shut down the connection." §7.2 (line 186) has the kernel mint exactly such a credential — "a short-lived, signed attribute snapshot… issued once per session/task and re-validated on TTL expiry or attribute drift" — but specifies no countermand path and no locus for detecting "attribute drift." Line 242's failure table ("Kernel unreachable → every PEP denies. No cached-allow; a subject context past TTL is a denial") only covers post-TTL: inside the TTL window a PEP holding a valid subject context keeps serving after an attribute revocation or kernel outage, which is a bounded cached-allow in tension with doctrine #2 ("no cached-allow"). Naming the PA role is therefore not merely cosmetic — it is the hook that makes the missing revocation/countermand obligation visible. I would upgrade the *recommendation* from "optional" to "name PA and specify the countermand path + drift-detection locus," while leaving this finding's severity at discussion since its payload is a clean record.

RL#1 bearing: `abac-dcs-architecture.md` is dated 2026-07-15 and is NOT in the RL#1 scope list (README, KLC, container-architecture, autopsy, ADR-0001..0003, corpus commit `5e76b96`). Nothing in RL#1 concerned these citations, so "killed" is not defensible — this is new-document material. Being strict about relocation: the residual I surfaced above (a security property — revocation of a live subject context — asserted with no named detector or enforcement locus) is the same structural shape as RL#1 Class A, reappearing at a new seam in a new document. I record that as relocated_class so the design probe can reason about it, rather than letting a "clean record" verdict launder it.

findings.summary: The NATO findings warn that CUI has no direct NATO equivalent, may map to NATO RESTRICTED only by category, and that equivalence is a policy decision requiring approved SPIF rules — but §6.4 lists 'equivalency maps' as a SPIF input and treats coalition readiness as the same kernel with a richer lattice.
findings.evidence: 'Nothing in this deployment is a special mode: it is §8.1's kernel with a richer lattice' does not absorb the findings' authority-gate warning that classification equivalence is not a technical default.
findings.recommendation: Document CUI↔NATO equivalence as a policy-based, category-dependent mapping requiring approved SPIF rules before coalition content marked CUI may be enabled.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
VERIFIED AGAINST TEXT — but the finding is right for the wrong reason, and its framing is partly refuted.

What checks out (the residual, narrowed defect):
- `design/abac-dcs-architecture.md:158` (§6.4) lists "equivalency maps" as one field of the deployment lattice declaration ("levels, category sets, releasability communities, handling domains, equivalency maps") and never elaborates it again. Grep of the whole corpus (`grep -rn "equivalenc" design/`) returns exactly one hit outside the imported reference: that line. Nowhere in abac-dcs-architecture.md, knowledge-lifecycle-contract.md, or container-architecture.md is it stated that a classification-equivalence mapping is a policy decision requiring approval by a classification authority — the explicit ⚠️ WARNING at `design/references/nato-dcra-acp240-findings.md:602-605` ("Classification equivalence mapping is a policy decision, not a technical one … the rules themselves must be approved by appropriate classification authorities").
- The boot-validation battery (§9.1 item 1) checks only that the "SPIF lattice [is] well-formed (a valid partial order; category sets internally consistent)" — a *structural* check. Nothing binds an equivalency map to an approving authority or an accreditation artifact.
- The corpus already owns the exact pattern it failed to apply here: §6.5's restricted-category certification gate (undeclared → refused; declared-but-uncertified → loud, un-silenceable "NOT CERTIFIED" stamping; certified → accreditation reference recorded in Tier-0 silences it). Equivalency maps are precisely a "supported by schema, not yet authority-approved" surface, and they are not wired into that gate. That asymmetry — GDPR/PII/PHI get a certification gate, cross-policy classification equivalence does not — is the real defect.

What I refute in the finding as filed:
- The class label "equivalence-overclaim" is wrong. The corpus makes no CUI↔NATO claim anywhere. §2's status row (line 39) says STANAG 4774/4778/5636 + ACP 240 are only "schema-ready at MVP … ACP 240 conformance claimed only after the document is in hand (§14)", and §14 (line 313) records ACP 240 as "full text acquisition pending" with 4774/4778/5636 full texts "Not held". That is an authority-gate posture already present, and it directly contradicts "overclaim."
- The recommendation's premise ("before coalition content marked CUI may be enabled") does not correspond to anything in the document. §8.2 is a deliberately notional single-lattice SECRET//REL enclave with no US↔NATO label transformation and no CUI at all; the NATO findings' `transform_label` / cross-policy transformation capability is simply not claimed.
- The quoted sentence is misread. "Nothing in this deployment is a special mode: it is §8.1's kernel with a richer lattice and a stricter map" (line 218) is an assertion about *kernel architecture* (no coalition-specific code path), not about classification equivalence. It is a true and unremarkable statement; loading it with an equivalence claim is the misreading.

Adjacent tension worth naming (stronger than the filed finding, not filed): §3 item 4 (line 106) declares "one lattice per deployment; subject attributes and resource labels are both points in it. The SPIF (§6.4) is the single vocabulary source." An *equivalency map* is by definition a mapping between two vocabularies. §6.4 lists the field but gives it no semantics inside a one-lattice-per-deployment model and no compile target among the three surfaces (Cedar entities / RLS predicates / label validators). So the field is either vestigial vocabulary carried over from the MCP's `labeling/spif.go` port, or an unstated second-vocabulary escape hatch from the single-vocabulary invariant. Either way the fix is one edit: state what an equivalency map is, whether it compiles anywhere, and gate it behind §6.5's certification mechanism (uncertified equivalence map → loud persistent warning; certified → recorded accreditation reference), with §9.1 checking presence of that reference rather than only partial-order well-formedness.

Severity re-assessed down to **discussion**: no security property is currently mis-stated or defeated (there is no equivalence machinery to defeat), no conformance is overclaimed, and the design is at v0.2 with Phase B explicitly holding the 4774/4778 work. This is an under-specified Tier-0 field plus a missed reuse of an in-corpus gate — a one-paragraph edit, not an ADR. I would drop `adr_candidate` to false; if anything it is a line item on the existing Phase B / §14 gate.

Not an external floor: the seam is entirely inside the corpus's own control (add the sentence, extend §6.5). Nothing here terminates against an invariant outside the system.

findings.summary: The NATO findings treat STANAG 5636 core metadata as a mandatory trinity with 4774/4778, but core_metadata and NCMS discovery appear nowhere in the inventory or growth path while 5636 is listed as an Authority.
findings.evidence: Only 4774 label_id and OpenTDF binding are mentioned in the port.
findings.recommendation: Add core_metadata/NCMS discovery to a stated phase, or lower STANAG 5636 from Authority to 'planned authority (Phase C)'.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
Verified against the text; refutation attempts failed.

1. The premise is accurate. `design/references/nato-dcra-acp240-findings.md` §4.3 states 4774 labels and 4778 binding "Together they form the **mandatory metadata infrastructure** for NATO systems", and §8 quotes AC/322-D(2024)0166: "All data posted to shared data spaces **MUST** include metadata per STANAG 5636 (NCMS)". The same extract carries `MCP-NATO-03` (Priority: High) and a `core_metadata` table sketch (§ "New: Core Metadata Table (STANAG 5636 / NCMS)", ~L488) with Dublin Core fields, plus tool surfaces `get_core_metadata` / `search_by_metadata`, and places NCMS metadata in the "Walk" maturity tier.

2. The port genuinely omits it. `grep -n "5636\|core_metadata\|NCMS"` across `design/*.md` returns hits only in `abac-dcs-architecture.md` L39 (§2.1 Authority table), L266–267/L302 (4774/4778 only), and L317 (§14). `core_metadata` and NCMS appear **nowhere** in the architecture doc — not in the §6.1 inventory (L137, which enumerates the ported schema exhaustively down to `classification_confidence` and the 4774 `label_id` placeholder), not in the §13 growth path (Phase B names only "STANAG 4774 `confidentiality_labels` + 4778 binding tables"; Phase C names coalition JOINT/FGI/tetragraph workflows), and not in `knowledge-lifecycle-contract.md` or `container-architecture.md`.

3. Refutation attempt — "the §2.1 row already hedges." It does not hedge *this*. The answer cell reads: "Schema-ready at MVP (ported `label_id` placeholder); binding lands with OpenTDF (§11); ACP 240 conformance claimed only after the document is in hand (§14)". Every clause answers 4774 (label), 4778 (binding), or ACP 240. Nothing in the cell answers 5636 (discovery metadata), which is a different capability from labelling/binding — the row silently lets 4774/4778's answer stand in for a third standard.

4. Refutation attempt — "§14 covers the gap." §14 makes it worse, and this is corroborating evidence the conflation is real rather than a deliberate deferral: the row is "STANAG 4774 / 4778 / 5636 full texts | Not held | **Label/binding formats (§6.4, §11)**". 5636 does not feed label/binding formats at all — it is Dublin-Core-derived discovery metadata. So the one place that tracks the 5636 gap mis-states what 5636 is for, meaning no part of the corpus tracks the actual NCMS obligation.

5. Refutation attempt — YAGNI / deny-by-default legitimately excludes it. This partly succeeds on *substance* and is why severity stays low: discovery metadata is not an access-control primitive, and a deny-by-default kernel loses nothing by deferring it. But it does not refute the finding as stated, because the finding's ask is a documentation-honesty fix (phase it, or downgrade the Authority listing), not a demand to build it. The corpus holds itself to exactly this standard in the same table cell — "ACP 240 conformance claimed only after the document is in hand" — and elsewhere ("full texts pending lake ingestion (§14) — final design re-walks them"). Listing 5636 as an Authority with an answer that only covers its two siblings is inconsistent with the doc's own conformance-honesty discipline.

Severity re-assessed independently: **discussion**, unchanged. No enforcement gap, no trust-plane consequence, no schema rework implied — the exposure is an overclaimed conformance line plus a mis-mapped §14 reference row. It sits below the review's should-fix bar but is more than a nit because §14 (the explicit gap register) actively mis-describes the standard, so the gap is not merely deferred, it is untracked. Minimal fix: change the §2.1 answer cell to state 5636/NCMS discovery metadata is out of scope for MVP (or a named phase), and split the §14 row so 5636's "Feeds" reads discovery metadata rather than label/binding formats.

rl1_disposition: **new**. `RL1-design-review-2026-07-14.md` names two root-cause classes — Class A (enforcement asserted without a trust-plane locus) and Class B (two-representations drift) — and the 22-blocker docket contains nothing on 5636/NCMS or on the §2.1 authority table. findings.summary: The RS*/ES*-only allowlist is copied from BoringCrypto-era MCP evidence while Maknae switches to aws-lc-rs, without re-deriving which JWT algorithms are FIPS-allowed for that module.
findings.evidence: 'aws-lc-rs in Maknae's Rust perimeter rather than the MCP's BoringCrypto' alongside 'RS256/384/512, ES256/384 only; HS*/PS*/EdDSA/none rejected'.
findings.recommendation: Re-derive the allowlist against aws-lc-rs's FIPS-validated algorithm set and record the derivation rather than the copied list.
findings.verifier_reasoning: Verified textually. abac-dcs-architecture.md:123 carries the BoringCrypto-era allowlist (RS256/384/512, ES256/384; HS*/PS*/EdDSA/none rejected) in the same breath as announcing the module swap to aws-lc-rs, under a section header that self-declares the baseline "Adopted wholesale from the MCP's compliance record" (line 116). The defect I am confirming is the derivation/provenance defect (a module-specific rationale retained across a module change, undocumented), which is verifiable here independent of the external fact. External fact I cannot verify in this environment and that governs the *remedy* rather than the defect: exactly which JWS algorithms fall inside the AWS-LC FIPS module's validated boundary at the pinned version (whether RSA-PSS, Ed25519 under FIPS 186-5, and P-521 are in scope) — that requires the CMVP certificate. Severity stays discussion: no exploitable weakness (the list is a strict subset of approved algorithms, so nothing unsafe is admitted), but it is an unrecorded, unverified crypto-policy claim in a document whose whole posture is citable control mappings, and it can produce a false IdP-compatibility rejection. findings.relocated_class: Class B — two representations of one fact (data-plane instance, not the documentary instance RL#1 catalogued)
findings.summary: Memory is placed in two homes with no closed split rule: the Lake holds memory content and a co-located memory subsystem, while the state store holds the memory recall (FTS) index and subject-scoped personal-memory rows — with no statement of which bytes are authoritative or how the index is derived and kept consistent.
findings.evidence: 'memory content lives in the Lake' / 'memory subsystem co-locates with lake' vs 'the memory recall index (FTS)' in operational state and 'subject ownership… personal memory'.
findings.recommendation: Define the authoritative home for each memory concept, state that the FTS index is a derived projection of the Lake, and specify the consistency/rebuild protocol and its label handling.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
Half the finding is REFUTED by text it did not cite; a narrower residual survives.

Refuted half — "no statement of which bytes are authoritative." The corpus states the split rule explicitly and in more than one place:
- abac-dcs-architecture.md §3.1 (lines 77-78) draws the line by category: "**Governed knowledge** (documents, skills, memory content) lives in the Lake" vs "**Operational state** ... the memory recall index (FTS)" — content in the Lake, index in the store.
- Same section, line 82: "the Lake stays markdown — the state store never becomes a shadow knowledge base," which is precisely the never-authoritative-for-knowledge boundary the finding says is absent. It sits one sentence after the analogous Tier-0 rule ("materialized copy for joins, never the authority").
- container-architecture.md §3.9 restates the boundary as "Knowledge stays in the Lake."
- The "dual home" framing is also weak on its own terms: container §3.5 says the memory subsystem co-locates with `lake` because "both are labeled-markdown-plus-index stores" — one home for content, one for its index, which is the ordinary source/derived-index shape, not two co-equal homes.
- The "subject-scoped personal-memory rows" evidence is a misread. abac §6.3's "operator-owned rows (health, financial, personal memory) join against `handling_grants`" is an enumeration of *handling domains* motivating the `subject` column, not a claim that memory content is stored as rows. KLC §5 independently homes Memory in the memory subsystem.
- Label handling of the index rows is also already specified: §6.2 declares one logical schema with two projections and asserts "A label crossing from a lake document into a session row survives the projection change bit-for-bit"; container §3.9 requires the full DCS column set with `NOT NULL` label columns.

Surviving residual (verified myself). Nothing in any of the three documents states the **direction of derivation as an invariant** or specifies a **consistency/invalidation protocol** for the FTS index. Searches for "rebuild", "reindex", "stale", "consistenc", "projection" across all three files return only the SPIF/label-projection and KLC freshness material — nothing binding the memory index to its Lake source. This matters because KLC's own lifecycle makes the source *mutable in the security-relevant direction*: §9/§10 demotion on drift ("Stale: ... demote one tier"), the dreaming cycle's re-verification and consolidation (§8 step 4, KLC line 226), downgrade-by-signed-act (§6), and object deletion all change label/tier/existence of the Lake-side memory. An FTS index row carries a snapshot of the label and (for FTS, by construction) content tokens; with no propagation rule, a demoted, re-labeled, downgraded, or deleted memory can remain servable through recall against a stale row whose `NOT NULL` labels are stale-but-valid — RLS will happily enforce the *old* label. That is a hook-B disclosure seam, and it is exactly the "two representations that must agree" shape, only in data rather than prose. It is a patchable seam: a one-line invariant ("the memory recall index is a derived projection of the Lake; label/tier/existence changes propagate before the index serves, and the index is rebuildable from the Lake") plus a note on rebuild ownership closes it, in the same register as the existing Tier-0 and shadow-knowledge-base boundaries.

Severity: not should-fix as written, because the authority-home and label-projection parts of the recommendation are already satisfied and quoting them as missing overstates the gap. Downgraded to discussion — a genuine, security-adjacent omission at a document set that is otherwise explicit about exactly this kind of invariant, closable with a sentence rather than a redesign.

findings.summary: D7 states 'tokens assert identity only — attributes never ride in claims', yet the token still carries client scopes and §5.2 uses them as an authorization axis ('scopes gate what a client application may request') — scopes are claims that authorize, so the identity-only slogan overclaims.
findings.evidence: 'The token asserts identity only (iss+sub, session, client scopes)'.
findings.recommendation: Restate D7 to say attributes never ride in claims while scopes remain a distinct client-capability axis, and define how the two compose at the PDP — or remove scopes from the token.
findings.verifier_reasoning:
Verified the text. §5.2 item 3 (abac-dcs-architecture.md:131) reads: "The token asserts **identity only** (`iss`+`sub`, session, client scopes)." — so the parenthetical does enumerate client scopes inside a token labeled "identity only", and the same paragraph does use scopes as an authorization axis: "**Scopes gate what a client application may request; attributes gate what an operator may see. Two axes, never conflated.**" §16 D7 (line 353) compresses this to "tokens assert identity only — attributes never ride in claims". The literal wording defect is real: a scope is authorization data, not identity, so "identity only" is imprecise on its face.

But most of the finding's force is refuted by the corpus itself. (1) The class label "scopes-claims-axis-blur" does not hold — the very sentence cited as evidence of the blur is the sentence that forbids the conflation and names the two axes separately. The finding's first recommendation ("restate D7 to say attributes never ride in claims while scopes remain a distinct client-capability axis") is already present verbatim in §5.2; only the one-line §16 decision-log row is compressed, and a decision-log row is a pointer to the normative section, not a second normative statement (the corpus's own READ-don't-RECONSTRUCT heuristic argues against expanding it into a restated copy). (2) The em-dash clause in D7 supplies the operative definition — "identity only" is defined by "attributes never ride in claims" — and the normative rule ("the kernel binds attributes from the Tier-0 store — claims in the JWT are never the attribute source", echoed at line 56 and mapped at line 35 to DoDI 8520.04) is unambiguous. No reader of this corpus could conclude scopes may substitute for kernel-bound attributes.

The residue that survives is the second half of the recommendation: "define how the two compose at the PDP" is genuinely unstated. §7/§9 enumerate Cedar decision inputs as (principal, action, resource=labels, context=environment attributes), and §4's environment class is explicitly time / network location / host-sandbox posture / channel origin (line 99) — client scopes appear in none of them, and no PEP is named for scope enforcement. However, §5.1 inherits the MCP's implemented OAuth 2.1 / RFC 9068 / RFC 8707 baseline wholesale (13/13 RFCs, references/oauth-compliance.md), under which scope validation is ordinary resource-server token validation at the gateway boundary, prior to and independent of the Cedar evaluation. So the composition is largely determined by the inherited baseline rather than left open — it is simply not restated here. That makes this a wording/completeness nit (one clarifying clause: scopes are validated at the RS boundary and can only narrow, never widen, the ABAC decision), not a should-fix design defect.

Not an external floor — a one-sentence patchable seam in prose, nothing outside the system's control. Not tied to an RL#1 blocker; B4 (gateway asserts identity) is adjacent but a distinct defect, so this is new.

refuted.summary: §7.3 asserts SET LOCAL GUCs are 'pool-safe; no attribute bleed between pooled connections' while §17 Q3 concedes pooler transaction-mode compatibility 'must be proven' — mis-pooled connections bleed subject attributes across operators.
refuted.reasoning:
Checked the actual text. §7.3 (line 194): "Subject attributes arrive as **per-transaction `SET LOCAL` GUCs** — pool-safe; no attribute bleed between pooled connections". §17 Q3 (line 369): "Connection architecture for the state store — per-service pools vs. a pooler (pgBouncer) given `SET LOCAL` transaction-scoped attributes; pooler transaction-mode compatibility must be proven in the vectors."

Three reasons the finding does not survive:

1. It misstates the external fact. `SET LOCAL` is reverted by the PostgreSQL server at transaction end (commit or rollback) — that is a server-side guarantee, not something a pooler can defeat. In pgBouncer transaction mode a server connection is pinned to one client for the duration of a transaction, so a `SET LOCAL` value cannot be observed by another client; this is precisely the documented reason `SET LOCAL` is the recommended idiom under transaction pooling (as opposed to plain `SET`, which does bleed). Cross-operator *attribute bleed* therefore is not the reachable failure mode. The reachable failure mode is the opposite: `SET LOCAL` issued outside an explicit transaction block silently no-ops (warning only), or statement-mode pooling breaks transactions entirely — in both cases the GUC is absent, `current_setting` yields NULL or errors, and the RLS predicate returns zero rows. That is the *fewer-rows* direction §7.3 already claims and which the deny-all default policy and `NOT NULL` label columns reinforce.

2. The claimed §7.3-vs-§17 contradiction is a misread of what Q3 concedes. Q3 is an open *architecture* question (per-service pools vs. a shared pgBouncer) carrying a verification obligation ("must be proven in the vectors"). It does not say the isolation property is doubtful; it says the deployment topology is undecided and the chosen topology must be proven. Asserting a designed property while naming its proof obligation is the corpus's own conformance-spine discipline (§12, D15: "RLS-in-CI against real PostgreSQL"), not two representations of one fact that have diverged. Removing the "pool-safe" assertion, as recommended, would delete a correct and load-bearing rationale for choosing `SET LOCAL` over `SET`.

3. The recommendation is largely already in the corpus: §12 item 3 and D15 already require the generated RLS policies to run the identical vectors against real containerized PostgreSQL in CI, and Q3 already binds the pooler question to those vectors.

Residual (the only thing left, and it is small): §12's vector list describes setting subject GUCs against PostgreSQL directly and does not name a *pooled* execution path, so the pooler proof obligation is stated in the open-questions list without a corresponding named vector. A one-line addition to §12 (run the RLS vectors through the selected pooler, asserting isolation and that a missing/no-op GUC yields zero rows rather than an error-free wide read) would close it. That is a nit-grade coverage/wording gap, not the should-fix "unproven pooling claim" alleged.

Also worth recording for the merge: this was found only by grok (two lenses, one model family), and the specific mechanism it asserts — bleed across pooled connections — is the part that does not hold.

refuted.summary: Label validators are one of the three SPIF compile surfaces but appear in neither the §12 CI surface list nor the §9.1 parity check.
refuted.reasoning:
Verified the text directly. §6.4 (abac-dcs-architecture.md:156-164) does list three compile targets from the SPIF, and §12 (line 283ff) does enumerate only three CI surfaces (`maknae-dcs-core` + PyO3 bindings, the Cedar policy set, the generated RLS policies), with §9.1 item 5 covering only RLS-vs-database parity. So the surface-level observation is textually accurate. It nonetheless fails as a coverage gap on two independent grounds already in the corpus:

(1) §12 does not present its numbered list as an exhaustive registry — its governing sentence is universal: "**Every surface that touches labels passes the *identical* vectors in CI**", with the list as the instantiation. And §6.2 scopes exactly where validators live: "Same vocabulary, same lattice, both projections generated from `maknae-dcs-core`'s types" — the two projections named are YAML frontmatter on lake objects and DCS columns on state-store rows, i.e. precisely the "ingest and write-path schema enforcement" the §6.4 validator target describes. Validators are therefore inside CI surface #1 (`maknae-dcs-core` and its bindings), not outside the list. §12 also independently subjects that crate to property tests (monotonicity, lattice join, partial order) and mutation testing gated as release blockers.

(2) The §9.1 half misreads why the parity check exists. §6.4 says all three targets compile "from one file at kernel load". A parity hash is needed only where the compiled output has a *separately deployed external counterpart that can drift* — RLS predicates live in PostgreSQL, outside the kernel process, hence item 5; the Cedar policy set is separately authored data, hence item 4's conformance-vector check. Label validators compiled in-process at load from the single SPIF have no second representation to diverge from. Demanding a boot parity check for them would mean introducing a second stored artifact to hash against — which is the corpus's (and the operator doctrine's) "two representations that must agree" class, i.e. the fix would manufacture the defect. §6.4's closing claim ("zero drift by construction — divergence is a boot failure") is consistent: for validators the drift is eliminated structurally, not by a check.

Residual: the enumeration in §12 could name validators explicitly for readability, and one could argue codegen bugs in the validator emitter deserve a named vector line even if the crate is tested. That is an editorial precision point, not a coverage gap — hence nit, not discussion. No bearing on any RL#1 blocker (RL1-design-review-2026-07-14.md contains no validator or §12-surface finding; its Class B "two-representations drift" cluster, if anything, argues against the recommended fix's parity-check half).

external_floor: false — the residual is a wording seam inside the authors' control, not an invariant outside the system.

refuted.summary: Tier-0 signed configuration is deliberately copied into the untrusted-adjacent state store 'for joins, never the authority', yet §7.3's at-rest predicate performs exactly that join — with no refresh trigger, staleness bound, invalidation, or parity check, and the failure direction is more rows, not fewer.
refuted.reasoning:
I attacked the finding's two load-bearing claims against the text and both fail.

CLAIM 1 — "§7.3's at-rest predicate performs exactly that join [against the materialized copy]." Not supported. §7.3 (line 192) names the predicate as "dominance predicate over the classification ordinal + releasability array containment + `noforn` + `subject`/`handling_grants` join," and the very next line (194) specifies the source of the subject side: "Subject attributes arrive as **per-transaction `SET LOCAL` GUCs** — pool-safe; no attribute bleed between pooled connections." Read with §6.3 (line 151, "operator-owned rows … join against `handling_grants`"), the join is row-column `subject` × GUC-supplied `handling_grants` — resource attribute from the row, subject attribute from the kernel-minted GUC. No materialized subject-attribute table is referenced anywhere in the predicate.

CLAIM 2 — "the document never says whether handling_grants on the subject side comes from the SET LOCAL GUC or from the materialized table." Refuted three more times independently of §7.3: §12 item 3 (line 289) defines the CI conformance procedure as "insert labeled rows, **set subject GUCs**, assert exact row visibility" — i.e. the tested enforcement path takes subject attributes from GUCs; D9 (line 355) ratifies "Kernel-minted subject contexts … RLS plumbing: `SET LOCAL` GUCs"; and container-architecture.md line 70 repeats "`SET LOCAL` per-transaction subject attributes" as the state store's contract. Four concordant statements is a specified source, not an omission.

The finding's own primary recommendation ("require all subject attributes to reach RLS through the kernel-minted GUCs — one representation, nothing to diverge") is therefore already the corpus's specified design, which is itself evidence the finding misread rather than discovered.

WHAT SURVIVES (narrow, and not the claimed defect): §3.1 line 82 / §4 rule 1 line 103 license a materialized Tier-0 copy "for joins" without ever enumerating *which* joins, without prohibiting enforcement use, and without a staleness/refresh/parity spec — and the finding is correct that §9.1 check 5 (line 230) covers generated-predicates-vs-deployed-policies, not materialized-rows-vs-signed-store. So the residue is a contract-honesty/scope-statement gap in an untrusted-adjacent plane: an unqualified affordance that a future implementer could read as permission to source enforcement inputs from the copy. Verified each load-bearing claim against the text; the finding's evidentiary core is misread.

1. "The trust-model delta is undocumented." Contradicted at the exact sentence the finding quotes. `abac-dcs-architecture.md` §3.1 states the delta explicitly and gives the substituting mechanism: "In the MCP, the database made sense because the LLM never touches it; in Maknae the same property is achieved by construction — the runtime touches state only through the kernel's decisions," plus "The runtime plane is stateless by declared design ... working sets are checked in and out through kernel-mediated access." The corpus does not port the origin's trusted-writer assumption; it names it as non-transferring and replaces it.

2. "A trust class the origin schema never modeled." KLC §2 axiom 3: "No subject — including the agent runtime itself — is implicitly trusted. Retrieved content is treated as input from an untrusted principal until promoted." KLC §5's tier table is literally a write-authority-by-actor-class table ("Who can place content here": operator signature only / promotion pipeline / consolidation cycle / any authorized ingest, with "All new knowledge starts here" = Tier 3). KLC §11 opens "An agent that feeds itself has failure modes a curated lake does not" and gives four load-bearing anti-poisoning rules. KLC §15 encodes them as invariants (`tier_0_writes: operator_signature_only`, `tier_ceiling_raised_by_automation: never`, `derived_ceiling: min_of_inputs`, `classification_downgrade_by_automation: never`). Agent-generated content IS modeled as a distinct, weaker trust class — that is the tier axis's entire purpose.

3. "Whose columns carry no provenance distinction." Directly contradicted by `abac-dcs-architecture.md` §6.3 ("What Maknae adds to the MCP schema" — precisely the delta the finding says is missing): "KLC lifecycle axis — `tier`, `tier_ceiling`, provenance/lineage, freshness — orthogonal to classification (KLC §5 ruling: lifecycle answers 'how trusted is this object'; the lattice answers 'who may see it')", plus `subject` ownership and high-water-mark derivation. §6.2 puts those columns on exactly the rows the finding names (sessions, tasks, memory index, audit). The recommendation "model LLM-written rows as a distinct trust class with stronger provenance guarantees" asks for machinery the corpus already specifies.

The finding's class label ("ported-trust-model-nontransfer") is therefore wrong: nothing was silently ported. It reads §3.1's acknowledgement of the delta as if it were an unexamined inheritance.

RESIDUAL that does survive, and it is narrower and differently-shaped than the finding: the state-store's *write path* has no specified authority model. Layer 2 is described purely as read filtering ("injects label predicates into its queries") and Layer 3's stated failure mode is "always *fewer* rows"; the §7.3 plumbing list (SET LOCAL GUCs, FORCE RLS, no BYPASSRLS, deny-all default, NOT NULL labels) names no `WITH CHECK` clause and no per-table INSERT/UPDATE authority. `container-architecture.md` §3.9 says "access is SQL through layer-2 PEPs only" without saying which service roles may write which tables. Consequence: a caller holding a valid kernel-minted subject context can write a session row labeled *below* the true high-water mark of its inputs — the §6.3 "born labeled at the join" derivation is computed by the assembling code, not verified by the kernel or by a WITH CHECK predicate — and audit's "append-only" (§10) is asserted without a mechanism. That is not a new class: it is RL#1 Class A ("enforcement asserted without a trust-plane locus... invariants asserted over state the untrusted plane can write") relocated onto the state-store seam that the 2026-07-15 abac document introduced. It is a patchable seam (add write-side RLS `WITH CHECK` generated from the SPIF, per-role table grants, kernel-verified label derivation on write) and belongs in the ADR-0005 enforcement-locus work RL#1 already opened, not in a new "trust-model delta documentation" ADR.

Note: RL#1's scope (§Scope, corpus commit 5e76b96) did not include `abac-dcs-architecture.md`, so the finding's `rl1_disposition: new` is defensible for the *document*; but the underlying defect is Class A, not new.

(1) MCP origin — abac §6.1: "The complete `dcs` schema from the MCP ports as Maknae's label vocabulary — this is a port of a built artifact, not a new design." §2.2 scopes the imported `references/dcs-schema-migration.md` to "design rationale imported by reference, not re-argued," explicitly "for reviewers without MCP repo access." container-architecture §6 "Security MCP harvest" states its "decision logic is deliberately NOT linked as a library." No text makes the MCP a standing authority Maknae must track.

(2) Microkosmos origin — container-architecture §6 "Provenance of the crate" is a seed-and-lift-out plan: (a) factor into an in-repo lib crate with the existing suite proving behavior unchanged, (b) "lift the crate to its shared home once the public API stabilizes." The terminal state is ONE crate, not a maintained fork. Open item #5 scopes the pre-extraction survey. A one-time extraction with a lift-out step is not a two-representations seam.

(3) SPIF/Cedar/RLS/validators — the only genuinely live multi-surface case, and the corpus already: declares the single source of truth (abac §4 "The SPIF (§6.4) is the single vocabulary source"; §6.4 "One vocabulary, three surfaces, zero drift by construction"; §6.2 both projections "generated from `maknae-dcs-core`'s types … never hand-rolled"; §12 "Conformance vectors are the single spine"), and specifies fail-on-divergence gates (§9.1 boot check #5 generated-RLS-vs-deployed-policy parity hash, "drift is a boot failure"; §9.1 #4 vectors vs loaded Cedar policy set; §12 identical vectors in CI across the Rust crate, PyO3 bindings, Cedar policy set, and generated RLS executed against real PostgreSQL; container-architecture §6 "Bindings prevent re-implementation; vectors catch divergence anyway").

Both substantive asks in the recommendation are therefore already satisfied in the text, and the third (a sync protocol with the MCP snapshot and Microkosmos extract) asks for machinery for seams the design does not create.

Residual, nit-tier and already acknowledged: the in-repo MCP snapshot has no stated staleness/refresh policy against its upstream — but abac revision 0.2 already records "retention before public release is an open decision," and the snapshot carries rationale rather than normative vocabulary.

Note: the sharper live question in this territory is already on the record independently at design/reviews/RL-convergence-ledger.md:52 (RL#2 row) — whether the §9.1 parity hash and §12 vectors verify semantic equivalence ACROSS surfaces or merely each surface separately. This finding does not make that claim and supplies no evidence for it; it should not be credited as a Class B instance.

refuted.summary: §5.1 declares the companion compliance matrix authoritative and then restates the 13-RFC baseline as bullets — algorithm allowlists, DCR fences and FIPS lists that can desync from references/oauth-compliance.md and the live MCP record with no diff gate.
refuted.reasoning:
Checked §5.1 (design/abac-dcs-architecture.md:114–125) against the companion it is accused of summarizing (design/references/oauth-compliance.md).

1. NO ACTUAL DIVERGENCE EXISTS. Every value the finding names as drift-prone matches the companion exactly. §5.1's FIPS allowlist ("RS256/384/512, ES256/384 only; HS*/PS*/EdDSA/none rejected; enforced twice — parser config + post-parse check") is a verbatim-accurate reduction of companion §5.1/§5.2/§5.3 (permitted table: RS256/384/512, ES256/384; rejected table: HS*, PS*, EdDSA, none; "Algorithm enforcement is applied twice"). The OAuth 2.1 consolidated bullet matches companion §3.12's six-bullet list item-for-item (PKCE mandatory, implicit disabled, ROPC disabled, refresh rotation, bearer via Authorization header, exact redirect URI). The DCR-fence bullet and the RFC 8414/9728/9068/9110-9111 bullets likewise track §3.4–§3.11. Class B in RL#1 was grounded in copies that HAVE diverged (#42/#45–47, #55–58, all cited with the concrete divergence). No divergence is demonstrated here, and I found none.

2. THE "CANONICAL SOURCE" PREMISE IS MISREAD. The companion is not maknae's normative source. Its own header block (references/oauth-compliance.md:1–12) declares it "Copied verbatim from the operator's Security MCP Server repository… Treat this file as a read-only snapshot — the origin repository owns the living document. Evidence paths and internal links resolve only in the origin repository." It documents a DIFFERENT system: Keycloak as Authorization Server, Go/BoringCrypto, evidence file:line paths into another repo. §5.1 does not declare it authoritative for maknae's requirements; it scopes the pointer precisely — "per-RFC requirements, evidence, and NIST mappings live there" — i.e. detail lives in the companion, the requirement statement is maknae's. That is the pointer discipline the finding asks for, already applied, at the correct granularity.

3. THE TWO REPRESENTATIONS ARE NOT REQUIRED TO AGREE — which is what disqualifies the class. Class B is "two representations that MUST agree." Here maknae's baseline is deliberately allowed to differ from the MCP record and already does, in-line and marked: "`aws-lc-rs` in Maknae's Rust perimeter rather than the MCP's BoringCrypto" (:123), and §5.2 flatly contradicts the companion's architecture — "Maknae is never the Authorization Server" where the companion documents an AS. A diff gate against a frozen foreign-system snapshot would fire on intended divergence, not on defects. Also: a frozen snapshot cannot desync on its own, and the design does not bind to the live MCP record (§14 lists what must be re-walked before final design; the MCP compliance record is not among them, precisely because it is prior art, not authority).

4. THE FINDING'S OWN FALLBACK IS ALREADY SATISFIED. It concedes "or restate only the conclusions Maknae itself owns." §5.1 IS the conclusions maknae owns — a design doc that said only "see the companion" would make another system's implementation record normative for maknae, which is the worse defect and contradicts §5.2.

Residual (nit, and not the reported defect): the "adopted wholesale" framing inherits one rationale that does not survive the crypto-perimeter swap. The companion rejects PS256/384/512 and EdDSA on the explicit ground that they are "not included in Go BoringCrypto" / "not FIPS validated in BoringCrypto" (references/oauth-compliance.md §5.2) — a BoringCrypto-specific fact, not a FIPS-general one. Maknae swaps to aws-lc-rs, where the BoringCrypto-scoped exclusions do not automatically hold. So §5.1 carries forward an allowlist whose exclusion basis is tied to a module maknae is not using. That is an inherited-rationale-scope issue (a DIFFERENT class from summary-of-canonical, and one that a "make it a pointer" fix would entrench rather than fix), and it depends on aws-lc-rs's actual FIPS-validated algorithm set, which I did not verify against a CMVP certificate here. Worth raising separately; it does not rehabilitate this finding.

foundBy is a single grok lens (multi-representation) with merged_count 1 — a lens firing on surface shape (bullets near a pointer) without checking either the companion's declared status or whether any copy had actually diverged.

refuted.summary: The doctrine bullets restate KLC §2's fail-closed, lattice-bottom and single-PDP machinery in abac prose rather than pointing at it — a second copy of the doctrine that can drift.
refuted.reasoning: Verified directly against the text. The finding asserts ABAC §1's doctrine bullets restate "KLC §2's fail-closed, lattice-bottom and single-PDP machinery." Two of those three items do not exist in KLC at all: grep for "frictionless|lattice bottom|unrestricted|only PDP|one decision engine|fail closed|grace mode|cached-allow" across knowledge-lifecycle-contract.md returns ZERO hits. KLC §2's four axioms are Secure-by-Design/Default, DCS, Zero Trust, and Deny-by-default; there is no lattice-bottom doctrine and no single-PDP doctrine to be a second copy of. ABAC bullet 3 (lattice bottom is frictionless) and bullet 4 (kernel is the only PDP; N enforcement points, one at-rest floor) are original to this document — bullet 3/4 content is recorded as this doc's own ratified decision D10 (abac-dcs-architecture.md:356) and bullet 4 is the load-bearing premise of §3's ABAC decomposition table and §7's three-layer stack. Bullet 1 (breaches cut off at design stage, multiple independently-tested layers) is likewise absent from KLC. Only bullet 2 overlaps KLC at all, and only in one clause: KLC §2 axiom 4 "Absence of a rule is a denial" plus axiom 1 "no permissive mode" vs ABAC "Absence of a rule, an attribute, a label, a signature, or a reachable decision point is a denial... no grace mode, no cached-allow." Four of the five denial surfaces ABAC enumerates (attribute, label, signature, reachable decision point) are ABAC-domain-specific and appear nowhere in KLC, and ABAC drops KLC's epistemics scoping — this is extension, not duplication. Further, the very line the finding cites as the defect ("Doctrine, extending KLC §2", line 19) IS the pointer RL#1's recommendation asks for: it names the canonical section it extends, and the header's Depends-on row (line 9) links KLC as the authority for label schema/hooks/invariants. Where the doc does restate KLC rules elsewhere it points explicitly (line 244: "Rejected, never defaulted (KLC §6...)"; line 23 cites KLC §6 for unlabeled rejection). The finding concedes no divergence is measured; the residual is a one-clause wording overlap in bullet 2 ("no grace mode" vs "no permissive mode"), which is nit-grade at most and not the drift-prone duplication of normative machinery described. This is not an instance of RL#1 Class B, whose real cases (RL1 §3: hook table vs §15 invariants vs §6 prose; ADR-status desync; lake-model drift) all involve rules restated with materially divergent content.

refuted.summary: The inherited OAuth→NIST mappings satisfy AC-16/AC-3 via JWT UIAS claims and Keycloak AS controls, but Maknae removes claims-as-PIP and externalizes the AS — so those control satisfiers do not transfer without a rewritten evidence map.
refuted.reasoning:
The finding asserts Maknae "adopts the inherited matrix wholesale," including its AC-16/AC-3 evidence. The text does not support that, and the corpus already does exactly what the recommendation asks, in three places.

1. Scope of "adopted wholesale" (abac-dcs-architecture.md:114-116). The heading is "5.1 Inherited RFC baseline" and the object of adoption is the RFC set — every bullet that follows is an RFC/JOSE/operational item (OAuth 2.1 core, RFC 8707, 8414/9728, 9068, 7591+CIMD, JOSE FIPS allowlist, 9110/9111). "per-RFC requirements, evidence, and NIST mappings live there" is a parenthetical describing the *companion's* contents and location, not an assertion that those mappings are Maknae's evidence. No NIST control id is claimed anywhere in §5.1.

2. The companion is explicitly framed as another system's read-only snapshot (oauth-compliance.md:1-12): "Copied verbatim from the operator's Security MCP Server repository ... Evidence paths and internal links resolve only in the origin repository. Treat this file as a read-only snapshot — the origin repository owns the living document." Appendix A's "AC-16 | UIAS claims" is therefore on its face a statement about the MCP, not a Maknae satisfier.

3. The evidence map IS re-derived against Tier-0 binding, in Maknae-owned tables:
   - §15 (:325-338) maps AC-16 to "Subject attributes from authoritative signed store; no self-assertion" (with IA-2 and DoDI 8520.04 §3.4/§4.3), to "Labels travel with data ... SPIF single source" (AC-16, SC-16), and AC-16(6) to BLP dominance. AC-3 is mapped to three-layer PDP/PEP/RLS enforcement and to the RLS backstop — never to token claims.
   - Critically, the one §15 row that *does* cite the inherited baseline — "OAuth 2.1 identity front door (RFC baseline §5.1)" — claims **IA-2, IA-5(2), IA-8, SC-8, SC-13, SC-23 and deliberately not AC-16 or AC-3**. That is precisely the re-derivation the finding says is missing.
   - KLC §13 (:245-247) and ADR-0003 (:35-36) independently re-derive AC-3/AC-16 against deny-by-default Cedar, label-to-data binding, and BLP — none against JWT claims.

4. The mechanism divergence is not silent: §5.2 item 3 (:131) states "the kernel binds attributes from the Tier-0 store — claims in the JWT are never the attribute source. This is the deliberate divergence from the MCP (where uias_* claims ride in the token, making the IdP the attribute PIP)", and §5.2 item 1 (:129) states Maknae is never the AS. §3 (:56) and D7 (:353) repeat it. The "Adopted wholesale" sentence sits between these two statements.

The only residual is cosmetic: the §5.1 parenthetical mentions "NIST mappings live there" without a one-clause caveat that the companion's mappings describe the MCP's mechanisms and that §15 is Maknae's. Adding "(that matrix's control satisfiers describe the MCP; Maknae's own mapping is §15)" would close it. That is a wording nit under the corpus's own §0006 single-source doctrine, not a should-fix redesign of an evidence map that already exists.

I could not verify externally that the origin MCP repo's Appendix A is unchanged since import, but that does not affect the verdict — the drift claim fails on Maknae's own text regardless.

refuted.summary: Surface 3 describes identity→Tier-0 attribute binding, not an OAuth AS/RS/client role; labeling it an 'OAuth surface' launders a non-OAuth internal credential under the 13-RFC baseline.
refuted.reasoning:
Read §5 (5.1/5.2), §16 D7/D9, §17 Q4 of design/abac-dcs-architecture.md, plus the RL#1 review's blocker list.

The finding misreads §5.2 surface 3. Surface 3's actual text is entirely about the *inbound OAuth token* and what it may and may not carry: "The token asserts identity only (`iss`+`sub`, session, client scopes)… claims in the JWT are never the attribute source… Scopes gate what a client application may request; attributes gate what an operator may see. Two axes, never conflated." That is a constraint on OAuth artifacts (JWT claims, client scopes, the IdP-as-PIP anti-pattern from the MCP) — it is properly an OAuth-surface concern, and it is precisely the deliberate divergence D7 records ("tokens assert identity only — attributes never ride in claims").

The finding's premise — that surface 3 "describes an internal service credential (see §17 Q4)" — is not supported: §5.2 item 3 never mentions kernel-minted subject contexts or a service-to-service envelope. That mechanism lives elsewhere (D9 "kernel-minted subject contexts", §17 Q4 "Internal service-to-service credential format… JWT with RFC 8707 audience binding vs a bespoke signed structure; decide at kernel-skeleton time"). So the corpus already does exactly what the recommendation asks: the internal credential is held separately and explicitly marked *undecided*, with no claim of RFC-baseline inheritance. An open question cannot launder a baseline; §5.1's baseline is scoped to the OAuth front door, and no text extends 13/13 RFC coverage to the internal envelope.

What survives is at most a taxonomy nit: surfaces 1 and 2 are OAuth *roles* (RS, client) while surface 3 is a cross-cutting rule about token content, so "three OAuth surfaces" is a slightly loose heading. That is a wording preference, not a security defect, and does not warrant the recommended structural separation. Note also that if §17 Q4 resolves toward "JWT with RFC 8707 audience binding," the internal credential would legitimately sit under parts of the §5.1 baseline anyway — the doc is being cautious, not sloppy.

Not tied to an RL#1 blocker: the nearest neighbor is the RL#1 bound-gateway-trust item (identity→attribute resolution at an untrusted gateway boundary), which is a genuinely different defect about *who is trusted to perform* the binding, not about what the surface is labeled. This finding neither kills nor relocates it.

Not an external floor — this is a document-wording question fully inside the authors' control, so accept+document does not apply.

refuted.summary: The design says IdP attribute claims are never the attribute source but does not say whether unexpected attribute claims are rejected, stripped, or merely ignored — ignore-while-present lets operators believe the IdP is still the attribute source.
refuted.reasoning:
I read §4 (load-bearing rules), §5.2 item 3, the ABAC-role table (line 64), and the D7 decision-log row in design/abac-dcs-architecture.md.

The finding's stated harm is that silence about unexpected attribute claims "lets operators believe the IdP is still the attribute source." That harm is foreclosed by the corpus in four separate places: (1) §4 rule 1 — "Attributes live in the Tier-0 signed store … The gateway authenticates *who*; only the kernel binds *what they are*. **No self-asserted attributes.**"; (2) the ABAC-role table row "PIP — subject attributes … `gateway` asserts operator identity; **kernel binds attributes** from the Tier-0 signed store," explicitly contrasted with the MCP's "extracts UIAS claims from the JWT"; (3) §5.2 item 3 itself; (4) decision-log D7 — "tokens assert identity only — attributes never ride in claims." A reader cannot come away believing the IdP is the attribute PIP.

On mechanism: the architecture makes stray claims inert *by construction*, not by an "ignore" policy. There is no PIP that reads the token for attributes — the only subject-attribute PIP is the kernel binding from the Tier-0 signed store, and §6.4's SPIF is the single vocabulary source compiled into Cedar entities, RLS predicates, and label validators. A `uias_clearance` claim in an inbound token has no consumer anywhere in the described data path. "Ignored" in the finding's sense implies a code path that saw the value and declined it; no such path exists. This is the corpus's own READ-reality/single-representation posture — one authoritative attribute source, nothing to diverge from.

On the recommendation (reject tokens carrying attribute claims, or strip and audit): this is a defense-in-depth *addition*, not repair of a stated-vs-actual gap. It also carries an unpriced cost — Maknae is a Resource Server federating arbitrary external IdPs (Keycloak, Authentik, Dex, CAC/PIV enterprise IdPs) and explicitly "marries the RFC contract, never the IdP product" (§5.2 item 1). Hard-rejecting tokens with extra claims would fail against conformant IdPs emitting unrelated organizational claims, and needs a claim-name matcher the design otherwise doesn't need. §5.1 already rejects what matters for token integrity (FIPS algorithm allowlist enforced twice, mandatory RFC 8707 audience binding).

The surviving residual is an observability nit, not a design defect: since the SPIF already names the attribute dimensions from a single source, a deployment could cheaply *detect and audit* an inbound token bearing claims matching those names as a misconfiguration signal (an IdP admin who thinks they are granting clearance via claims). Worth one sentence in §5.2; its absence does not make the divergence "assumed rather than enforced" — enforcement is by absence of any consumer, which is stronger than a stripper.

No external fact is in play; this resolves entirely against the document text. It does not bear on an RL#1 blocker: Class A in reviews/RL1-design-review-2026-07-14.md is "kernel-attributed enforcement whose data path executes in the untrusted plane / PDP inputs sourced from less-trusted planes without kernel verification," and §5.2 item 3 is the element that *satisfies* that pattern for subject attributes (attribute path moved out of the token into kernel/Tier-0), not a relocation of it.
